SPREN BATTLE ABBEY

QUINCEY 

SAIRE de QUINCEY, the Surety, born before 1154, was a Baron present at Lincoln when William the Lion of Scotland did homage to the English monarch in October 1200. He obtained large grants and immunities from King John and was created Earl of Winchester, 2 March 1207, having been governor in 1203 of the Castle of Ruil in Normandy. He is credited with rewriting Magna Charta from the 

Charter of King Henry I and the Saxon Code. Because he had opposed the King's concession to the Pope's legate, he was bitterly hated by King John. One of the Barons to whom the City and Tower of 

London were resigned, Saire de Quincey was excommunicated with the other Barons the following year. He was sent, with Robert Fitz- 

Walter, the Surety, by the other Barons, to invite the Dauphin of France to assume the Crown of England and, even after the death of King John, he kept a strong garrison in Montsorell Castle in behalf of Prince Louis. When the Barons, being greatly outnumbered, were defeated by the troops of King Henry III, Saire de Quincey, with many others, was made prisoner and his estates forfeited. In the following 

October his immense estates were restored upon his submission. In 

1218 the Earl of Winchester went with the Earls of Chester and Arundel to the Holy Land, assisted at the siege of Damietta in 1219, and died 3 November in the same year, on the way to Jerusalem. His wife was Margaret Beaumont, whom he married before 1173.

At the beginning of John's reign Saire de Quincey was not a Baron, much less a great one. In the civil war the King had had the advantage over the rebels. Few of the Barons had had much actual military experience. The Barons' contribution to the war was the scutage they paid, a war fund substituted for the contingent of knights owed to the King's service. The money was collected from vassals, and mercenary knights were paid from it. Many of the mercenaries were regulars who served the same Baron from campaign to campaign, but those Barons who are known to have had extensive military experience were only Saire de Quincey, Robert FitzWalter, William de Mowbray, William d'Albini, Roger de Cressi and Robert de Roos.

Saire de Quincey is associated with two stalwart Castles in the South of England: Colchester and Winchester, both with the Latin castrum root, signifying that they were once the sites of Roman forts. 

Colchester Castle could not have been built before the early 12th Century, though Roman materials may have been re-used in its construction. The keep, the only portion now surviving, is in complete harmony with other Norman castles. Colchester must have been a

formidable stronghold, and a challenge to Saire de Quincey. The 

King's men held the Castle against Quincey, the first Earl to attack Colchester. John had given the fortress into the charge of a Fleming whom he thought he could trust. But Quincey took the Castle, and later found holding it more difficult. The fighting was of such a nature that John himself came to Colchester to see just how stubborn Saire de Quincey was. The Earl held the Castle for two months, but lack of food forced him to give up and take flight to France. 

Colchester was the largest Norman keep in England. It measures one hundred fifty-two by one hundred seventeen feet, enclosing nearly twice the area of the Tower of London. Its walls vary between eleven and thirty feet in thickness. It was erected either by William the 

Conqueror or by William II. It is of the quadrangular variety, turreted at the corners. In it and elsewhere herringbone masonry has been noted. 

Winchester Castle was first erected by William the Conqueror.

Later alterations and extra height were added by Henry III, about the year 1138. The great Hall has Purbeck columns of 13th Century architecture, supporting a restored roof and containing handsome windows of the same approximate period. Only the keep remains. "How commonplace this saying, 'Only the keep still stands,' thanks to the old builders who made the keep strong and high to withstand time, and so difficult to tear down that it escaped the looters of the ages." Perhaps Murphy was thinking of Colchester or Winchester when he thus wrote, for this was the fate of the Quincey strongholds. 

ROOS The Barons de Roos owned Helmsley or Hamlake Castle. Baedeker remarks only that it is an interesting Castle, but we can give some description of it. Hamlake has a rectangular bailey, a barbican, and an outwork at the East end of the bailey. Its singular defense was a double line of ditches, both of which were fed by the River Rye. The curtain wall was built about 1170, and the keep about 1190. The 

East gateway and barbican are ascribed to the 13th Century. The 

Castle, except for the keep, was destroyed in 1649. The other half remains, one hundred feet above the bailey. The keep is an excellent example of traditional design, combining the old square style with coming roundness in towers. The outside of the tower is rounded to baffle sappers, and the portion inside the curtain is square, as a convenience for the occupants.

ROBERT de ROOS of Fursan, the Surety, fourth Baron of Hamlake Manor, was born in 1177. When only fifteen years of age he had paid a thousand marks' fine for livery of his lands, and in 1197 when aged twenty years, while with the King of Normandy, he was arrested, though we know nothing of the offense, and was committed to the custody of Hugh de Chaumont. However, de Chaumont trusted his prisoner to William de Spiney, and the latter allowed him to escape out of the Castle of Bonville. King Richard thereupon hanged de Spiney and collected a fine of twelve hundred marks, about eight hundred pounds, from Roos' guardian as the price of his continued freedom. 

When John became King, he gave young Roos the whole Barony of his great grandmother's father, Walter d'Espec, as conciliation. 

About the 14th of King John, Robert assumed the habit of a monk, whereupon the custody of all his lands and Castle Werke, were committed to Philip d'Ulcote. But Robert did not long continue as a recluse, as in about a year he was executing the office of high sheriff of co. Cumberland. At the beginning of the struggle of the Barons for a constitutional government, he at first sided with King John and, in consequence, obtained some valuable grants from the Crown. He was made governor of Carlisle, but was later won over by the Barons. He returned to his allegiance in the reign of Henry III for, in 1217/8, his manors were restored to him, and, although he was a witness to the second Great Charter and the Forest Charter of 1224, he seems to have been in favor with the King. 

Roos erected the Castles of Helmsley, or Hamlake, in Yorkshire, and of Werke, in Northumberland. He was a member of the Order of Knights Templar. He died in 1226/7 and was buried "in his proper habit" in the Knights' Church, or the New Temple in London, where his tomb may be seen. His effigy is described by Gough, in "Sepulchral Monuments," as "the most elegant of all the figures in the Temple Church, representing a comly young knight in mail, and a flowing mantle with a kind of cowl; his hair neatly curled at the sides; his crown appears shaved. His hands are elevated in a praying posture, and on his left arm is a short, pointed shield charged with three water-bougets. He has on his left side a long sword, and the armor of his legs, which are crossed, has a ridge, or a seam up the front, continued over the knee.At his feet is a lion, and the whole figure measures six feet two inches." He married Isabel, daughter of William the Lion, King of Scotland, and widow of Robert Bruce.

SAYE 

GEOFFREY de SAYE, the Surety, was in arms with the other Barons against the King, and consequently his extensive lands and possessions in ten counties were seized. These were given to Peter de Crohim. Six of the counties we can name: Northampton, Cambridge, Essex, Norfolk, Suffolk and Lincoln, but we cannot be sure of what Castles in those areas were Geoffrey's, or which other four counties he could claim.

While William d'Albini and his companions were holding Rochester Castle, they had been assured that other Baronial leaders would relieve them if the Castle were to be besieged by King John. 

Such a rescue would not have been easy unless the Royal guards were lax in watching the bridge over the Medway. If this bridge were under guard, a march to Rochester from London along the Dover Road would prove impossible, the company then being forced to detour and approach Rochester from Maidstone. Nevertheless, on 26 October, they moved in as far as Dover, where they soon heard that the King was on his way to meet them. They promptly returned to London, leaving the Rochester garrison to do the best it could. 

Perhaps the march on Rochester was a sop to the Barons' consciences. Had it been a serious move, it would have been an extraordinarily foolish one. The only other attempt to save Rochester was negotiatory. On 9 November King John issued letters of conduct for 

Richard de Clare, Robert FitzWalter, Geoffrey de Saye and the Mayor of London, to confer with the Royal emissaries: Peter de Roches, Hubert de Burgh and the Earls of Arundel and Warren. There is no certainty that these men ever met. If indeed they did, nothing came of it. We suspect that the meeting was originally planned with the hope that a proposal would be accepted, and it is not unlikely that the proposal would have been a willingness to surrender Rochester Castle to the King if the garrison could go free, but no such move resulted. 

Yet despite the futility of the meeting, at least we see Geoffrey de Saye connected, if lightly, with Rochester Castle. And this is the only Castle with which we are able to link his name. 

Geoffrey de Saye returned to the Royalist party when the civil war was over, and sided with King Henry III, thereby regaining his lost lands after the expulsion of the Dauphin. He died 24 October 1230, leaving a son, William, as his heir, by Alice, daughter of William de Cheney.

CHAPTER 262 – SURETIES AND CASTLES 

2429 VERE 

The principal residence of the de VERES was Castle Headingham. 

The keep still stands sentry guard over the River Colne in the North of Essex, probably erected by Aubrey de Vere, who died in 1194. The 

Headingham keep ranks with that of Rochester as the finest of the square keeps in England.

Oxford Castle was the seat of the Earls de Vere. It now consists of little more than a Norman tower which stands inside the walls of a county jail. It was here that King Stephen laid siege to Matilda in 

1141. She escaped by a rope ladder fashioned from bed sheets during the night and, fleeing, found refuge at Wallingford. 

Oxford Castle is thought to be the oldest in all England. The 

Norman structure was built in 1071 by Robert d'Oilly. From what is left of it we can conclude that it was originally a pre-Norman motte and bailey fort. After the 1071 rebuilding, alterations were made by 

Henry II, between 1165 and 1173. He added the houses inside the shell keep, and also the well. He presumably built the diagonal keep on the motte, the foundations of which were discovered in the 18th 

Century. 

ROBERT de VERE, the Surety, born after 1164, became heir to his brother, Aubrey de Vere, who died without issue before September of 1214, and who was reputed to be one of the “evil councillors” of King John. Although he was hereditary lord great Chamberlain of the kingdom, Robert pursued a different course in politics from that of his brother, and became one of the principal Barons in arms against King John, a party to that covenant which resigned the custody of the City and Tower of London to the Barons, and one of those excommunicated by the Pope. In the beginning of the reign of King Henry 

III, after he had made his peace with that young monarch following the Battle of Lincoln, Robert was received into his favor, and was appointed one of the judges in the Court of King's Bench, but he died only a few months afterward, 25 October 1221, and was buried in the Priory of Hatfield, Broad Oak, in Essex. His wife was Isabel, who died 

3 February 1245, daughter of Hugh, second Baron de Bolebec in Northumberland.

VESCI 

The VESCI family had control of Alnwick Castle (pronounced "Onick") built as a threat to Scotland in Northumberland. The Vesci family came to an end, and the Castle went to the Percys in 1309. It

is now in fragments, embodied in a palace of later date. The walls have been integrated into the residence of the Dukes of Northumberland. The property consists of five acres. Fortunately, parts of the building have been restored. The oldest of these is the Norman gateway, dating from the 12th Century, also the well in the keep. 

In the second half of the 18th Century more than half the Castle was renovated, and an Italian style of decoration was applied to the interior. In the park there is a monument commemorating the capture of William the Lion, when he besieged the town in 1174.

According to the chronicler of Alnwick Abbey, the Barony of Alnwick belonged to Gilbert Tyson prior to the Conquest. His son and heir, William, was killed at Hastings, leaving no issue. His daughter and estates were granted to Ivo de Vesci. In 1297 William, first Baron Vesci, died without surviving issue, and left the Barony to the Bishop of Durham, who sold it to Sir Henry Percy. The Castle slowly became the center of the town, which supposedly received its borough charter from King John.

Alnwick Castle, built by Eustace FitzJohn in 1140, is said to be the finest example of its kind. It is one of those Castles that boast an open or shell keep and a complete enceinte. For two Centuries it remained tenantless until the present family succeeded. The restoration was instituted between 1750 and 1786. 

Near Philadelphia, the mansion of the Harrison Estate, now Beaver

College, Glenside, Pennsylvania, is a replica of the Castle of Alnwick in Northumberland. It is considered a very creditable facsimile. 

EUSTACE de VESCI, the Surety, was feudal lord of Alnwick Castle. He came of age in 1190 and, in 1199, was sent by King John as one of the ambassadors to King William the Lion of Scotland. He married one of William's daughters. Soon he became closely connected with the rise and progress of the Baronial cause. In 1212 he and Robert 

FitzWalter, the Surety, were called to give security for faithful allegiance, whereupon they fled to Scotland. De Vesci's English posessions were seized and also his Castle of Alnwick, which was to be destroyed, but the order was never carried out. This order so embittered de Vesci that he became the most persistent of the King's enemies, and a principal leader in the insurrection. He soon was taking a prominent part in all their conventions, endeavoring to revive the laws of Edward the Confessor. He was one of the Barons to whom the City and Tower of London were committed. He was excommunicated, and was one of those who urged the Dauphin to come to England. 

While attending his brother-in-law, Alexander, King of Scots, as he

CHAPTER 262-SURETIES AND CASTLES 

2431 welcomed Prince Louis and paid him Scotland's homage in 1216, Eustace de Vesci passed Bernard Castle in Yorkshire and noted that it displayed the Royal banner. He approached the Castle to see if and how it could be captured, and was mortally wounded in the attempt. 

WINDSOR CASTLE 

1 119 

Two Residences of Royalty 

When King John ruled England there were two Royal residences: 

Windsor Castle, twenty-one miles from London, on the Thames, and Corfe Castle on the Isle of Purbeck, co. Dorset, by the Sea. We know little about Windsor until Edward III came to the throne. It had always been the Royal residence, but in William the Conqueror's time it was not where it is now, nor was it in the days of King John. 

WINDSOR CASTLE 

Edward III is considered to have been the chief builder of Windsor Castle. We are told that at old Windsor there was a wooden Anglo- 

Saxon building predating Edward's structure. We assume that Edward was undertaking much reconstruction, perhaps on a Norman building, for he was in the process of restoring St. George's Chapel. Marshette 

Chute, in her delightful book, Geoffrey Chaucer of England, (New 

York, 1946) tells us that: "In addition to his regular duties as Clerk of the Works, Chaucer was given a special commission to oversee the repairs that were scheduled for St. George's Chapel at Windsor. This was the Chapel in which the Knights of the Garter did reverence to their patron saint,

and it had highly decorated walls, a great alabaster table before the high altar, and two volumes of French romances chained within the Chapel. King Edward had finished what he called this 'Chapel of convenient beauty' only four years earlier, and it was already in such a state, according to the commission appointing Chaucer to his task, that it would fall to the ground unless speedily repaired. “Chaucer left . . . after having served the King as his building superintendent for just under two years. He left his file of sixteen vouchers with the clerks of the Exchequer, and he turned over to the new Clerk of the Works a large pile of stone he had collected from Reigate and Stapleton to repair St. George's Chapel, which was now stored ready for use in the great hall at Windsor. Chaucer was responsible no longer for seeing that the gay little Chapel did not fall to the ground."

Edward the Confessor had granted Old Windsor to Westminster Abbey, but it was recovered by William the Conqueror for two other manors. William erected the Castle about two miles North of the village within the manor of Clewer, which was to be the nucleus for 

New Windsor (See J. E. Tighe, Annals of Windsor, London, 1858).

We also hear that William purchased the land for New Windsor outright from the monks of Westminster Abbey. 

Windsor Castle is now one of the most outstanding edifices of its type. It is situated high on a hill, where it flaunts its massive towers. 

Its great Round Tower, now somewhat higher than in Edward's day, can be seen almost anywhere in the surrounding country. From various points in the Park the fortress may be seen at the end of an avenue of stately trees, and when the sky is clear and the battlements streaming the Royal standards stand out in hard outline against it, it seems as though the pageantry of Edward's day were still alive. 

There are a number of stories told of John's tenancy of Windsor. 

One is the gruesome tale of William de Braos' wife, Matilda, imprisoned in the Round Tower, with a sheaf of wheat and a slice of raw bacon as the only food offered to her and her child. When the guard opened the door eleven days later, the two were found dead. 

According to Sidney Painter, chroniclers agree that Matilda Braos and her younger son, William, were starved to death, but that her older son escaped. The confinement was the end of a long chase and varied chicanery, for John was determined to capture the acid-tongued Matilda at all costs. Previously John had seized some Baronial fortresses and, in his interdict of 24 March 1208, had put himself in such a position as to be kept in constant fear of the plots of the disaffected

Barons. He therefore demanded hostages of the men he suspected. 

When his men approached Matilda saying that her sons were forfeit, she tartly replied that she would not give her sons to the man who had murdered his nephew. After that moment the Braos family were continually running from the King's men. 

Another episode in the life of John at Windsor is his prelude to his Normandy campaign. He summoned a great council to meet with him at Northampton. Gerard de Camville, sheriff of Lincolnshire, and 

Reginald de Cornhill were to send two tuns of wine to the King at Windsor, presumably to sustain him at the meeting. Reginald was also to send the King a "Romanicum Historie Anglie," literally, “a Romance of the History of England," probably an English history in French, no doubt a highly exaggerated account of the daring deeds of old. 

But the description would have led Reginald to what was wanted. John apparently wanted to ply his guests with wine to make them convivial, and then regale them with the tales of their heroic ancestors. The picture of King John, readying himself for the council with two tuns of wine and a history book, is indeed picturesque. 

CORFE CASTLE 

On the Isle of Purbeck, a small peninsula of Southern Dorset, at its very center, stands Corfe, one of the most remarkable of the English Castles, built on an enormous mound. Before its gates stands the village of Corfe, an aggregate of cottages seemingly huddled beneath the ruin that towers above them. The entrance to the Castle stands high above the cottages, and the main portion of the fortress has foundations higher than the gateway. The enclosure is cut off from the village by a deep fosse, crossed by a higher arched bridge. From inside the curtain one sees the Castle proper. Masonry lies strewn about like glacial debris. Walls, towers and buttresses rear up like cliffs, softened by an occasional arras of ivy. So ruined is the structure that experienced archeologists have had trouble in restoring the original ground plan. 

Even the keep, the one portion that in most castles, has defied time and destruction, here is shattered. One slice of the full height of the Great Tower stands alone, a splinter of a mighty donjon, looking like a chimney of a fire-gutted house. Corfe Castle is now in such a state that one is at a loss to distinguish one apartment from another. 

According to King John, Corfe Castle was as nearly impregnable as any Castle could be. Certainly its strength must have surpassed the average, for the Castle claimed a great advantage, both in position and structure. Not only had John made it his country residence: it was

his second Royal Court, and to its stout fastness he entrusted the Crown treasure. The ruins of Corfe date, for the most part, from the 

Norman period to the reign of Edward I. 

Matters did not run well for Prince Arthur at Corfe. Arthur was the son of John's elder brother and, according to the opposition, was the rightful heir to the Throne. He had become the pawn of those who had failed to keep John from seizing the Throne for himself, a Throne for which they felt moderately sure he had plotted murder. 

Arthur took up arms against John to no avail, for Arthur, his sister 

Eleanor and some two hundred knights were taken prisoner. Arthur was murdered, and Eleanor and the knights were imprisoned at Corfe. 

With Eleanor were two daughters of the King of Scotland who, for a little time, brightened her days behind those dark walls. 

But if the lot of Eleanor, the “Beauty of Brittany," and the two hundred, was sad, the cowardice and cruelty in the execution of a selected twenty-two was horrifying. John had these men sent to Corfe with instructions to the keeper of the Fort that he must carry out whatever oral instructions the Royal messengers gave. John apparently did not have the courage to write out his order and set his Seal to it, but rather let the appearance of ruthlessness fall on someone else. The messengers ordered that twenty-two of the knights were to be thrown into the strongest cells and were to be systematically starved to death. 

This form of liquidation seemed to have had the strongest appeal to the King.

Such is the picture of the two Royal Castles which were the homes of King John, and in which he confined and starved those who displeased him. Windsor, the House of Kings since pre-Conquest days, was perhaps a neighbor to a Royal seat a few miles removed some hundred years before, and has been the home of Royalty without interruption until the present day, whereas Corfe Castle, the seacoast retreat, where William d'Albini waited in chains after his garrison had been starved out of Rochester, is a windswept scene of desolation and mighty ruin.

In the article on English castles in the National Geographic Magazine, 1947, the author points out that it is significant that there is much left of the great cathedrals, that most of their beauty still remains. Buildings erected for worship and inspiration have stood, but the military works, even the strongest, are scattered bits of masonry, a single tower or a grass-covered mound. Bats and owls haunt the castle towers, but choirs still sing in naves seven hundred years old.

THE TOWER OF LONDON 

The motte for the Tower of London is an elevation, now called Tower Hill, on the East side of the City, on the North side of the Thames. It is now said to have been an ancient British stronghold. 

Tradition has it, however, that the first founder of the Tower was Julius Caesar, and remains of Roman fortifications have been found underneath the present site.

The fortress covers a roughly hexagonal tract, surrounded by a ditch once fed by the Thames. The ditch is now dry. Two lines of fortifications surround the inner bailey in which stands the keep, known as the White Tower, with its four turrets. It was built by 

Gundulph, Bishop of Rochester, about 1078. Its towers are of the early type, square like Colchester's. The outer circuit measures 1,050 yards. In some places the double curtain walls are forty feet high and twelve feet thick. The inner ward was formerly known as the 

Royal Quarter. It was defended by twelve great towers, spaced at irregular intervals. The outer ward was known as the Folks' Quarters. 

Since this was a Royal and a National stronghold, the King's officers probably held the inner bailey, while the outer served as a rallying place for the common soldiery, later John's mercenaries. 

The White Tower is typically Norman. It was commenced at the behest of William the Conqueror in 1078, and completed thirty years later. The original design was planned by Bishop Gundulph. 

Its length is one hundred sixteen feet, its width ninety-six feet, and it is ninety-two feet high, in three stories. Even though Christopher 

Wren refaced it and radically altered the windows, enough of the original remains to convince the spectator that this is indeed a noble product of the 11th Century, and the Lion Gate reminds him that in those days there was a menagerie under the Middle Tower, which was maintained until the middle 19th Century. 

Here  and Geoffrey de Mandeville fought their lawsuits, while under indirect fire from King John in the year 1212.

The Mandeville family had claimed an hereditary custodianship of the Tower since the 11th Century. However, no strong King had ever honored the claim.

The safety of the Tower meant the safety of the City. The King's garrison held the Tower, but the City soon fell into the Barons' hands. 

By 17 May 1215 the King could have crushed the rebellion, but did not do so in order to impress the Pope. Had the Tower been out in the open country, the rebel host would have been short-lived. So few were the actual fighting men among the Barons that John's mer-

cenaries would soon have made short work of them, but inside London's walls, aided and abetted by its citizens, the Barons were in a position to defy a strong army for a long time. 

As to the old problem of the ownership of the Tower, its extreme military importance made John loath to relinquish it, and he postponed consideration of the Mandeville claim. Meanwhile the Tower was given into the keeping of Cardinal Stephen Langton and he continued to hold it while the Barons resisted the King in London, following the meeting at Runnemede. The Tower and the City were key points. 

The Tower was the military heart of the Capitol, and was therefore even more important to the King than Windsor. The issues during this phase of the Baronial wars were the possession of London and the position of the Barons in relation to the Crown.

CHAPTER 263 The Reformation 

A concise summary of the Reformation is found in "A Reformation Sunday Message" by the Rev. Floyd E. Brown:

In his biography of Martin Luther, entitled "Here I Stand," Roland Bainton makes the observation that the Protestant Reformation was like a man climbing in the inky darkness of the stairway of an ancient cathedral, and in the blackness he reaches out a hand to steady himself and finds that his hand has caught hold of a rope. And he is startled to hear, at the end of the rope, the loud clanging of a bell. 

You remember how it happened. It was All Saints Eve in the year 

1517. A young Augustinian monk . . . with conscience outraged at a church which had been blatantly corrupt, which had usurped the authority of individual conscience, which had abused the very essence of the Christian faith... nailed to the Cathedral door at Wittenberg ninety-five propositions for debate . . . theses which struck at the very heart of that ancient church. 

And even though Martin Luther had no intention of starting any new movement in the life of the church, within a very few weeks his action was applauded throughout the land... for men everywhere had heard the ringing of that bell! It has been ringing now for more than four hundred years, until today there are hundreds of millions of Christian believers of Protestant persuasion. 

In essence, the Protestant Reformation was a reaction against the misrepresentation of the Christian faith by the medieval church. It all began in the soul of an outraged Augustinian monk who for years had sought a personal encounter with his God by rigidly disciplining his body, by the mortification of his flesh, and by giving himself to a meticulous observance of the precepts of his church. But in all this his soul remained barren and he was beset with spiritual dissatisfaction. 

But as he read his Bible the truth of God began to catch hold, until one day he came upon a truth in Paul's letter to the Romans that completely revolutionized his entire outlook. For there on the pages of the Scripture he read and understood "that the just shall live by faith” . . . that man's relationship to God in Christ was a personal spiritual experience, not at all dependent on what you did, but rather on what you were. And from its very inception the Protestant Reformation insisted that every man have the right of private judgment in matters spiritual; that every man have the privilege of reading God's 

Word and of interpreting it as the Holy Spirit illumined his under- 2439

standing; that every man seek his God in a personal redeeming encounter with Jesus Christ.

When speaking of the Reformation in England people sometimes express the opinion that it would never have come about if Henry VIII had not wanted another wife. Certainly Henry's affairs and his desire for a male heir became entangled with anti-Papal sentiments, but it was by no means the beginning of the Reformation in England. 

One is tempted to say that the English Reformation was part of an intellectual and religious unrest that smouldered in several parts of Europe. We need only count the names of Huss, Calvin, Zwingli, Luther and Knox to show that it was widespread; but England had its own problem long before the Renaissance, a state of development which brought the Reformation into being through the promotion of individual discovery. Actually the seeds of England's own conflict in religion are to be found in her age-old quarrel with France. 

Edward III, on the advice of Parliament, assumed the title of King of France, and war broke out anew in 1369. The antagonism was of the same type as that which had continued from 1351 to 1366. 

In 1305 the Pope resided at Avignon and, although Avignon was not considered a legal part of France, there was no doubt whatever that the King of France had control of it. While the Papacy suffered its removal from Rome, the English looked upon it as a tool for French politics. Meanwhile the Papal Court gave itself more and more to luxury and vice, and the cost of its wordly pleasures seemed to be coming from English coffers.

There was a system of provisions whereby the Pope might appoint his nominees to English benefices and expect that these benefices would be held by his appointees to the exclusion of other patrons. In 1351 the Statute of Provisions attempted to put an end to this system but, not being successful, it had to be re-enacted several years later. In 

1353 the Praemunire Statute was passed, in which an attempt was made to stop suits from being carried to foreign courts. The Statute was aimed at the action of the Papal Court at Avignon. Finally the Popes were claiming that England owed them 1,000 marks a year, and this was a symbol of King John's vassalage and a burden of dishonor. Since 

1333 Edward had had the government in his own hands and the payment had not been made. In 1366 Parliament declared that such payment would not be made.

CHAPTER 263 – THE REFORMATION 

2441 Meanwhile John of Gaunt, time-honored Lancastrian, was siding with those who protested against the wealth of the clergy and the corruption of some of them. The most popular writer of that period, Geoffrey Chaucer, shows us contemporary vignettes of the less admirable sort of churchman: the fun-loving sportsman, nominally a monk; the greasy friar, who will do anything for money; the pardoner, who sells indulgences and the allegedly miraculous relics of the saints, the actuality of which, as well as their miraculous nature, being equally suspicious; the summoner, who brings the erring up before the Ecclesiastical Court. All these conditions of church people are possible only in a system that has so deteriorated that any sort of vicious or lazy person may be found among the lesser lights. There are, of course, a hard-working and penniless parson, a witty priest and the sweet, childlike prioress. 

Against such abuses the voice of John Wycliffe was heard crying.

He had been a distinguished doctor at Oxford, and it was he who attracted the Duke of Lancaster's attention, through his argument against the Pope's claim to King John's feudal levy. In 1374 he went to Bruges to argue about provisions with Papal representatives and, in 1376, proposed to issue a book, On Civil Leadership, in which he maintained that, by altering feudal law somewhat, one could validly say that all men held their possessions in feoff from God. At the end of tenure mortal vassal may justly say, “All things come of Thee, O Lord, and of Thine own have we given Thee." Thus dominion is founded on grace, and the continuance of man's right to his possessions depends upon his remaining in a state of grace. 

In 1378 the Papacy divided and, for nearly a century and a half from that date, there were two Popes, one at Avignon and one at Rome. 

By now Wycliffe's respect for the Papacy was considerably less than it had been in the days of a single Pope. Wycliffe was now devoting himself to a translation of the Bible into English, "that might be understanded of the people." He was also busy heading his evangelistic program, which sent the "poor priests" about England preaching the Gospel to those who had no knowledge of Latin; and thus Wycliffe was led into controversy with the priesthood. His "poor priests" had seen much clerical pretension, and Wycliffe and his followers began to question the doctrines on which their authorities were based. 

By 1381 Wycliffe had stated his disbelief in the doctrine of transubstantiation, declaring that priests could not "make the body of Christ," a power which priests had claimed. By tearing at the very

heart of established dogma, he took the chance of losing many of his followers. 

Twenty years later matters had not improved. The clergy demanded more and more power. Ecclesiastical courts could name a heretic, but had no power to burn him. In England, Wycliffe died a natural death. On the Continent, John Huss went through the flames to his death. The House of Lords was filled with bishops and abbots. 

The House of Commons still envied the wealth of the Church, and had no sympathy with heresy. The statute for the burning of heretics, De heretico Comburendo, ushered in what little-feeling England had in common with the Inquisition of the Mediterranean nations. The first victim was William Sawtre, a priest who saw no change in the bread at Mass. He was burned before the law was even enacted. 

The year 1413 saw Henry V no longer the "Madcap Hal" but a responsible statesman, turning his thoughts toward the religion of his forefathers. He founded three friaries, and set out to crush the 

Wycliffe Lollards who preached against transubstantiation, auricular confession, the use of images, the selling-and sometimes the issuance of indulgences-and all in the speech of the laboring man. The Lollards claimed as their chief supporter Sir John Oldcastle, who bore the title of Lord Cobham in right of his wife. He was brought up before Archbishop Arundel. The Archbishop quietly asserted the necessity of preserving the traditional teaching. Oldcastle, equally calm, mentioned the falsity of its oldest doctrines. He was excommunicated, but little else happened, for Sir John Oldcastle silently disappeared. Meanwhile his followers, becoming enraged, plotted against the King's life and, early in 1414, there was a skirmish in St. Giles Fields, in which Henry's men assailed the rebels. Many escaped, but those who did not were burned or hanged; and another statute was formed, advocating harsher treatment of Lollardry, a name which denotes the tares (Latin: lolium) in the Church's wheat, which they considered themselves to be.

By the middle of the 15th Century ecclesiastical power had been considerably weakened through the race for power with France, and the constant erosion of the Wars of the Roses. Lollardry had faded with the death of Sir John Oldcastle, for that knight was publicly executed. The services of the Church were performed without the fervor that had filled them in the 13th Century. Chivalry was practically dead; that which remained of it was a romantic curiosity. The skies were glowing with the embers that were to flare up and become the Renaissance.

CHAPTER 263 2443 

– THE REFORMATION 

The next step was the climax of the Reformation, the reign of Henry VIII. From then until the beheading of Charles, England was to remain a cauldron of boiling religious controversy; and many a devout person was to go to the stake or block under Henry and, for opposing reasons, under Mary. As we have seen, Henry did not instigate the Reformation, but it was useful in allowing him to live as he wished. By the time Henry came to the throne the Renaissance spirit was a growing reality. In Italy it had been well under way for more than two centuries, even though in Italy the scholars held Christianity in contempt. In England there was no such breach. The 

English intellectual tried to revise his old faith in the light of contemporary ideas. Of the new reformers of the Universities, Thomas 

More is the most remarkable. He had hoped for great improvements under Henry, but was disillusioned when the King proceeded to become involved in war with France. Henry could brook no challenge to his will, but he overlooked people who did no more than disagree with him. He enjoyed the society of well educated men and urged 

More to take office under him. More refused for a time but, in 1518, feeling that Henry might accept his ideas, he became Sir Thomas More, Privy Councillor.

While More combined the Renaissance interest in humanity with a reverence for God and strove to mellow the older religious teaching, others threw off all religious restraint, and turned their thoughts to selfish enjoyment, or perhaps the pure refinement of their intellects. 

In Italy the Popes were victims of the era. Alexander VI indulged in the most flagrant of vice, and helped make the name of Borgia a shameful one for all time. Julius II became a temporal conqueror. 

Leo X was a connoisseur of art, but cared nothing for the ways of the soul. It was he who linked the spirit of Renaissance art with the 

House of the Medici, from which he came. The Papacy, he held, should be enjoyed to the fullest by those who were so fortunate as to have that post and, with this attitude so outspokenly stated, the Popes became no better and no worse than other powerful Renaissance princes. 

Meanwhile Wolsey, the Chancellor, deplored the Church for more practical reasons, notably the large number of uneducated men in the clergy. With the consent of the King and the Pope he started the dissolution of several monasteries in 1524, and used the money thus obtained to found two great colleges, one at Oxford and one at Ipswich. Henry, sympathizing, went so far as to accept no authority other than God. "We are by God's grace King of England," he said, "and have no superior but God. We will maintain the rights of the

Crown like our predecessors; your decrees you break and interpret at your pleasure, but we will not consent to your interpretations of them any more than our predecessors have done." Had the King been in the position of Henry II, he would at once have made a split with the Church; but Leo X was too much of this world, and did not let Henry's bluster and threats disturb him.

A religious revolution soon sprang up in Germany, drawing Henry and the Pope together. A Saxon friar, one Martin Luther, see elsewhere, was an eloquent preacher of morality, and the proponent of a doctrine which had long been laid aside. Justification by faith was his principal tenet. Luther taught the importance of individual faith, of man's personal relationship with God, and the nonimportance of the intervention of human beings between man and God. Luther's doctrine touched all human activity and breathed the spirit of political as well as religious liberty. 

Henry wrote a book denouncing Luther, for Henry prided himself on his knowledge of theology, and thus wrote, defending the seven sacraments. Since Luther was antagonistic to royalty, he answered 

Henry with scurrilous invective. The Pope was overjoyed. Henry was an influential champion and, for his pains, was awarded the title “Defender of the Faith." Had Henry been moved by a motive weaker than controversial vanity, he would have been secure in the Pope's approval until the end of his life. 

Henry, however, desired a son, for he had no surviving male heir. 

He wondered if he might rid himself of his present queen with the plea that marriage with his brother's wife was unlawful. Catharine of

Aragon was five years his senior, and he was tiring of her. In 1511 he had, in his diatribe against Luther, assigned a divine origin to the Papacy, but had told More the secret reason for the pronouncement: possibly because he might move the Pope to grant him a divorce, particularly if he could prove that it might mean a peaceful succession. In 

1555 he became more eager for the divorce, for it was then that he met a beautiful sixteen year old girl named Anne Boleyn. Since Anne would have nothing to do with him outside the bounds of marriage, Henry set his heart on divorce. Wolsey tried to make him abandon the project, foreseeing many complications; but no one could gainsay 

Henry, and Wolsey went about carrying out his master's instructions, though not with any joy. Suffice it to say that morals were the least of 

Wolsey's concern, but he did hold a strong political objection, for England was in danger of losing her alliance with Catharine's nephew, Emperor Charles V, if the divorce were accomplished. By now, the

CHAPTER 263 – THE REFORMATION 

2445 furor had become hopelessly entangled with Henry's political and personal commitments.

In 1532 the Commons set upon the Clergy, and Henry was behind them. The outcome was that he forced Convocation (Canterbury) to sign a document called the Submission of the Clergy, which simply meant that the officials of the Church could make no decision and act upon it without the King's permission. He now had the Clergy in such a position that it was impossible for them to protest against the divorce. Through this action Henry lost the best of his statesmen. 

Thomas More had been appointed Chancellor, as a replacement for Wolsey, in 1529. His Utopia had been written before Luther had made his break with the Papacy. When More took office he soon learned the extent to which his tolerance would have to be strained. Protestantism, as the Lutheran teaching was now called, had just begun to penetrate England, and was espoused by a handful of individuals. Certain persons who had not been satisfied with reasons already provided for the workings of the universe, turned to the teachings of justification by faith, while some of their comrades fell to berating the Clergy. 

Some few merely reviled the common creed of most Englishmen, and justification by faith led to a doubting of the merit of good works and even to a scornful contempt for them. 

More could not bear the bitterness of this turn of events. He tormented the critics with argument and ridicule, and used his authority to back the Clergy in stamping out heresy. He did not have grounds to fear that the King's increased authority would bring on a true revolt, for he knew Henry to be a typical man of the times, with no liking for heresy. But More could foresee that Henry's layman's mind might not always keep the faith of his fathers in sight. The ideas of the age were seething, and the current was strong. To men like 

More, only the Papacy would have the strength to withstand change. 

Henry had not attacked yet, but attack was soon to come and, in 1532, More retired rather than be involved in the coming revolution. 

It was now time for Henry to take direct steps with the Papacy, and his efforts found success for, by the end of 1532, Parliament had issued the Act of Annates. Annates were the first year's income of ecclesiastical benefices. This Act decreed that Annates paid to the Pope were to be kept back, but the Act was not to be enforced until the King had ratified it. This Henry did not do, hoping to threaten Pope 

Clement financially and keep him in suspense. But Pope Clement was not to be moved. Henry could wait no longer, and was secretly married to Anne Boleyn, 25 January 1533. He resolved to put an end to

Papal jurisdiction so that he could declare his former marriage null and void. If England were still bound to the Papacy, the injured wife could appeal to the Papal court. Thus came about the Act of Appeals, which declared the King to be the supreme authority in England. All temporal matters were to be decided by temporal judges, and spiritual matters by spiritual judges, but no appeals should be suffered to any authority outside the realm.

A convenient tool for Henry's national policy was found in Thomas Cranmer, whom the King had appointed Archbishop of Canterbury in the Spring of 1533. Cranmer was intellectually acute but morally weak, and was prone to ride with Henry's will. He had been active in Henry's divorce proceedings. In March he was half driven, half persuaded, to declare Catharine's marriage to be void and, in May, in the Archepiscopal court of Dunstable, he pronounced sentence against her. In accordance with the Act of Appeals the sentence was final. 

To forestall any move Catharine might make, Henry and Cranmer kept from her the exact day when the sentence would be given. The temporal benefits the Pope derived from England were at an end, as well as his spiritual jurisdiction. In July the Act of Annates was ratified by Henry VIII. 

The teachings of Zwingli, the Swiss reformer, spurred on the desire for stronger measures against heretics, for the Swiss preacher held that the sacramental bread and wine were merely symbolic. Amongst the persecuted was John Frith. He denied any belief in the doctrine of transubstantiation. He was burned at the stake. 

Hugh Latimer, the King's favorite chaplain, tended to test things by their moral worth, rather than by conformity to an intellectual standard. Pilgrimages, worship of saints and the idea of Purgatory seemed immoral to him, but his wish was to purify opinion, not to change it. He had the King's support, for he was made Bishop of 

Worcester in 1535.

On a wider scale the Reformation may thus be summed up. It was far more than a matter of English power politics. First of all, the 

Papacy was dangerously weakened during the Babylonian Captivity. 

The Renaissance Popes became so worldly that they were known as the secular Popes. There were altogether too many appointments to the 

Roman curia, leading to bribery and to the sale of bishoprics and other offices, an offense known as simony, all of which became an offense to temporal princes. Some bishops were more secular than spiritual and were in active conflict with the Papacy. Many of the regular parish priests were ignorant and unfit for spiritual leadership

CHAPTER 263 - THE REFORMATION 

2447 in an increasingly progressive society. The wealth of big monastic estates aroused envy in the hearts of secular leaders and, in England and Germany, these had no scruples against seizing them and breaking them up. Many Christians regarded only the empty form of their worship. Greater ambitions were aroused in new monarchies. Democratic sentiments were flowering in the ruins of the Middle Ages. 

Democratic forces aligned themselves with new monarchies to overthrow feudal lords and check Papal power. Rediscovery of classical culture nourished neo-paganism, while geographical discoveries increased materialism, and many other factors entered in to make man assert himself—to explore rather than to accept, to appeal to the God who had made him as well as all mankind.

The sale of indulgences was a prime scandal. An indulgence technically is "the commission of temporal punishment due to sin after its guilt has been forgiven, which the Church grants from the treasury of the merits of Christ and His saints." (See New Catholic

Dictionary). These spiritual benefits were sold on a wholesale scale throughout Europe and particularly in Germany. Pope Leo X was encouraging new ornamentation on St. Peter's basilica, and granted the privilege of selling indulgences to bishops on a percentage basis. 

Some bishops needed money to maintain armies and courts. Sales of indulgences took place in the manner of a public auction on the streets, agents peddling them and selling them for whatever they would bring. Pious men were heartbroken to see the faith thus degraded, and business people were angered at seeing so much money going to Rome and being drained from so many communities. 

In the England of the 16th Century horror had been spread by tales of the Inquisition. To many the Roman Church symbolized a system in which children informed against parents, according to which arrests were made on the grounds of spite, and torture or execution were common with scarcely more than a mock trial, after an admission of guilt had been extracted under pressure. 

Science enters the picture, presenting the sharpened eyes and ears of investigation and research. Science requires liberty for these pursuits, and the scientific spirit opposes the idea of “revelation" in its most rigid sense. Science does not mix with the supernatural. Its only authorty is the desire for truth.

Finally, the Bible had been translated into the vulgar tongue. It was studied in the original. Texts were compared and studied. Textual criticism was injected to oppose the accepted theory of a supernatural and infallible document. Now that a man was learned enough to

read and could make out and interpret most of the Bible for himself in his native language, authority was losing even more ground. 

The church officials were corrupt. Justice under the Inquisition had been cruelly parodied. Mental expansion had caused Englishmen to rise to a vigour which would no longer tolerate such degradations, such unfairness. The time had come when Englishmen, fired with the enthusiasm for geographic and scientific discovery, would assert themselves. Henry's private desires and political fears brought about the first real rift between England and Rome, but the English Reformation had not been kindled simply by a monarch's desire for a new wife, nor was the desire for a new wife merely a manifestation of royal lust. 

It is obvious that there had been political and religious dissatisfaction with Rome for two centuries before Henry's time, and in Europe the Albigenses had suffered even earlier. Unrest in England grew and diminished over the years, but with each new outburst the feeling had been more intense and reprisals more severe. Monasteries were to be looted for the national treasury, and there was more to come after the initial first step of Henry's reign. Henry's Litany, written in the English vernacular, was to become the nucleus for Edward's Prayer Book. Tyndal and Coverdale were to translate the Bible, and Tyndal was to become a martyr to the cause. There was to be controversy over the distribution of the Bible, for in the hands of radicals it might be come a dangerous weapon, at least the cause of many a bitter dispute. 

Then Mary's reign would come, glowing with blazing faggots, and hideous with the stake, block, whipping post, stocks and gyves with which the defeated party tried to coerce men back to the fold in the name of God. And indeed these brutalities set the seal on English religious independence. Nothing could have turned away the populace so forcibly as threats and torture. England had feared the possibility of an Inquisition, and now with the actual appearance of Inquisitorial cruelty and the threat of the overlordship of a rival seapower, men turned their backs on doctrine dictated from a foreign country on religion associated only with barbarity, and on their half-Spanish 

Queen and her cold Spanish consort.

Henry did not upset the religious and political structure of his kingdom solely for Anne Boleyn. It was his seriousness of purpose in his desire for an heir that caused him to raise such a tempest in his domestic life, and with both Church and State. The fact that his choice of another wife caused turmoil that set the pace for England and everyone influenced by her from that day is not denied, but that fact is but a portion of the picture. England's future did not rest upon

CHAPTER 263 - THE REFORMATION 

2449 Henry's whim. The sweep of two hundred years' growth made it easier for Henry to perform an act, personal by nature, for a national reason. 

Yet detractors of English Protestantism will, in the future, as they have in the past, say that the English Reformation was the result of Henry's encounter with a pretty Lady in Waiting.

MARTIN LUTHER IN HIS STUDY MARTIN LUTHER 

Born at Eisleben, Lower Saxony, 10 November 1483, Luther discovered about 1503 in the Library of the University of Erfurt a Latin Bible, and found to his no small delight that it contained more than the excerpts in common use. (The clergymen of that time knew only the Gospels and Epistles.) In 1505 he entered the Monastery of the 

Augustines at Erfurt. In 1507 he was consecrated priest, and in 1508 was made Professor of Philosophy in the new University of Wittenberg. 

In 1510 he visited the Court of Pope Leo X at Rome, on business connected with the Order. This journey revealed to him the irreligion and corruption of the clergy at Rome, and destroyed his reverence for the sanctity of the Pope.

He became a preacher at Wittenberg, and in 1512 was made a Doctor in Theology. His profound learning, together with the fame of his eloquence, soon made Luther known to the principal scholars and esteemed as a powerful advocate of the new light which was breaking upon the world. Great, therefore, was the attention excited by his ninety-five propositions given to the world 31 October 1517, and intended to put an end to indulgences by the Dominican Tetzel. His propositions were condemned as heretical as soon as they appeared. 

In 1520 Luther and his friends were excommunicated. His writings were burned in Rome, Cologne and Louvain. Indignant at this open

act of hostility (after his modest letter in which he had shown himself desirous of reconciliation, declared his submission to the Pope, and advised a reform in the Church). Luther burned the bull of excommunication and the decretals of the Papal canon at Wittenberg 10 December 1520. By this act he dissolved all connection with the 

Pope and the Roman Church. A few months later he was summoned by the newly elected German Emperor, Charles V, before the Diet of Worms and resolved to go in spite of all the remonstrances of his friends. Before the Emperor, the Archduke Ferdinand, six electors, twenty-four dukes, seven margraves, thirty bishops and prelates, and many princes, counts, lords and ambassadors, Luther left Worms, a conqueror; but it was so manifest that his enemies were determined on his destruction that Frederick the Wise conveyed him privately to 

Wartburg to save his life.

Neither the Emperor nor the Pope could disturb him in his retirement, of which he took advantage to translate the New Testament into German. This retirement lasted only ten months. When informed of the disturbances excited by Carlstadt on the subject of images he could no longer endure restraint. He hastened to Wittenberg, and the sermons, which he delivered for eight successive days after his return, in March 1522, to quell the violence of the enraged insurgents in Wittenberg, are patterns of moderation and wisdom and popular eloquence. 

Amidst these disputes and attacks his plans were matured for a total reformation in the Church, which was called for by the voice of the nation. In 1523 at Wittenberg, he began to purify the liturgy from its empty forms and, by laying aside his cowl in 1524, he gave the signal for the abolition of the monasteries and the better application of the goods of the Church. 

Against his will his adherents styled themselves Lutherans and engaged in a war which broke out immediately after his death and desolated Germany. As long as he lived Luther was for peace, and he succeeded in maintaining it. He regarded it as impious to seek to establish the cause of God by force; and during thirty years of his life the principles of the Reformation gained a firmer footing and were more widely propagated by his unshaken faith and unwearied endeavor than by all the wars, treaties and councils. 

Luther, in company, was always lively and abounded in sallies, wit and good humor, preserved in his “Tabletalks." He wrote hymns: 

Ein Feste Burg. A Mighty Fortress Is Our God. His fondness for music: he sang and relaxed playing on the flute and lute.

He spent

CHAPTER 263 - THE REFORMATION 

2451 some hours each day in meditation and prayer and was always accessible to visitors.

In 1525 Luther married an abbess, who had left her convent, Katharina von Bora, whom he dearly loved. They had six children, two of whom died at an early age. He died at Eisleben, 18 February 

1546, in his sixty-third year, and was buried in the Castle Church of 

Wittenberg. His wife died in 1552.

Luther completed for the people of Germany the translation of the whole Bible, with some assistance from Melanchthon and other friends, and thus rendered his name immortal. From 1526 to 1529 he prepared a new church service agreeable to the Gospel under the patronage of the Elector and with the aid of Melanchthon and other members of the Saxon Church. His larger and shorter Catechisms, to be used in schools, were also of great service. 

CALVIN 

John Calvin the second great Reformer, was born at Noyon, Picardy, 10 July 1509, and died 27 May 1564, at the age of 55 years.

He married at Strasburg in 1539 a widow, Idelette de Burie. They had one son who died early in life. His wife died in 1549. 

John Calvin had a sister, Catharine Calvin, who married William Whittingham of the City of Chester, a Puritan who fled from England to the Continent during the reign of Queen Mary and became pastor of the first Congregational Church at Geneva, where the wedding took place. They were the great, great grandparents of Martha Whittingham, who married in 1691 the Rev. John Rogers, a descendant of John 

Rogers the Martyr, ancestors of many representative American families. 

John Calvin's chief doctrines were: predestination; particular redemption; total depravity; irresistible grace; and the certain perseverance of the saints.

The followers of Calvin in Germany are called the Reformed. 

In France most Protestants are Calvinists. Calvinism is the professed belief of the greatest part of the Presbyterians, the Particular Baptists in England and India (1937) and the Associated Baptists in America, the Independents of every class in England and Scotland and the Congregationalists of New England. Wesley in England was Arminian and 

Whitfield was Calvanistic.

In Scotland, John Knox joined the Protestant party and preached in Dundee, Perth and St. Andrews, and St. Giles, Edinburgh.

In Ireland for various reasons the Reformation never made much progress.

Gustavus Adolphus, the pious King of Sweden, was used under God in saving the Reformation from complete ruin. Says an historian, "So far as the human eye can see, the Reformation, except for Gustavus Adolphus, would have been crushed in Germany, and probably in all northern Europe with the exception of England." It was during the

CHAPTER 264 Who Wrote Magna Charta? 

Often the question is asked: Who wrote Magna Charta? Before we answer, let us in turn ask how this is to be construed. Are they asking who penned it? Do they mean who planned it? Are they looking for an author? The Declaration of Independence was written by 

Thomas Jefferson. The literary style has been marked as his. He was the spokesman for its organization. If we look behind the typical prose of the times we may see, or imagine we see, the imprint of a personality. 

Truly the Declaration is an august work of prose and worthy to be remembered for the dignity of its cadence. It is for these reasons that phrases of it haunt our subconscious memories. Can we observe the 

Great Charter in such a fashion?

The answer is yes, but we shall not see the same sort of performance. Times had changed between the final framing of these two documents. The Middle Ages set no great store by authorship per se or personalities behind the news. It is assumed that twenty-five copies of Magna Charta were originally written, and by hand. They were not engraved as were the Declaration and the Constitution. Four sealed copies of Magna Charta are preserved-two in the collection of Robert Cotton, and one of these discovered in Dover Castle was badly damaged 2453

by the Cottonian fire. The third copy remains at Salisbury Cathedral where it has stayed from the first. The fourth and best preserved is the Lincoln copy.

As we have been told many times before, the Charter is contained on a single sheepskin or parchment, measuring seventeen and a half by eighteen inches. Its surface appears shriveled and darkened, but the writing is still clear, whatever the original composition of the ink -nut-gall or cuttlefish dye (sepia). On this one parchment there are some 3000 words, the average for a terse magazine story. The words are cut down to half their size. Latin case endings have been dropped. 

Abbreviations have been made with the aid of symbols denoting the syllables omitted. Some words have been run together. It will be noted too that the document has been started in a big bold hand, and that the writing gets smaller and smaller as the scribe tried to squeeze in just one more word at the end of the line or to sandwich in that last syllable so that the word would not have to be broken. It is a long trip for the eye, from the right-hand edge back to the left-hand edge and the beginning of the next line. 

Watch also the way the hand changes and turns at times to a scrawling cursive. The hand was getting cramped and tired. The quill pen needed trimming with a pen knife. The light from sputtering torches or a candle was dim indeed. There's much weariness in this writing, and it was done quickly as twenty-five copies had to be on hand. Though the initial maneuver had been previously thought out, John had been trapped and the scriptorium had to have the document written out so that the heralds in the halls and the priests in the abbeys could intone the endless rise and fall of the periods, stopping only for breath. When such a pause was made, we come to the end of a sentence, a full stop and a renewal with a capital letter exactly as in modern usage. Where there is a new division, an item, or where modern editors number a special provision, the reader-scribe takes no notice of the break if it starts with a relative pronoun or a pronoun introducing a subjunctive.

We note that the beginning of Article I, "Quod Anglicana Ecclesia libera sit" (that the English Church shall be Free) is run in with the preceding sentence. The writer, feeling that there was no such break here, wrote it as he would have read it aloud and doubtless muttered each word as he wrote it. Indeed, so prevalent was this practice that rules are found for scriptoria, telling the monks to read softly lest the combined mumbling of a whole writing workshop get on the nerves of serious scholars. As for the dropping of case endings, medieval imagina-

CHAPTER 264 - WHO WROTE MAGNA CHARTA? 

2455 tion provided an imp who gathered up all the case endings dropped by a priest at Mass. These were placed in one big hamper and the load was used to weight the scales against him on the Day of Judg. ment. We trust that the writer of Magna Charta has been forgiven his lost endings, that every Article might be included. 

When John was asked to review the Charter, we can be sure that it was not quite the same document as the one we now know. The 

Barons presented him with some sort of written piece which was later revised. After receiving John's imprint, the whole thing was drawn up into a formal charter. There was a document submitted to John, drawn up by Langton and Pembroke, but it seems likely that John approved of little or none of it, and by this time it was too late for it to matter much what he thought about it. The differences between Magna 

Charta and this earlier document rest only in minute details. 

Of course King John did not sign the document by spelling out his.name; he sealed it with hot wax, and the print, "data per manum nostram," not for the sake of custom as Barrington says, but because he and his courtiers could neither read nor write. 

The Seal itself is a matter of some interest. It seems that in 1212 the Great Seal was not always in constant attendance upon the King, and charters are known to have been issued at Westminster while the King was wandering about the realm. Apparently witnesses had to swear that they were present when a document was sealed in the King's absence. For his periods of travel John used the Privy Seal to seal letters, instructing the keeper at Westminster to apply the Great Seal to certain other important documents. He had reason to believe that there were conspiracies against him. Fearing that the Great Seal might get into the wrong hands, he devised complicated countersigns included in letters, ordering certain courses of action known only to himself and to the recipient (such as the showing of a certain ring) to show that his message and his alone had been received. It sounds childish, this method of registered delivery, but "uneasy lies the head that wears a crown."

We can see, therefore, behind the nervous script of Magna Charta, signs of human beings at work. Who were they? Was it one of the 

Barons who wrote this noble Latin "Concessimus etiam omnibus liberis hominibus regni nostri, pro nobis et haeredibus nostris in perpetuum, omnes libertates subscriptas, habendas et tenandas eis et haeredibus suis de nobis et haeredibus nostris?" Was this written by even an illiterate Baron, who being learned only in war, could read at the most the set phrases of legal documents, or the cliches of religious literature,

whose spoken tongue was French with a modicum of English for the servants? Could such a man write, and to what extent? Would he know the rigid medieval laws of rhetoric? The only scholar present was Richard de Gilpin, secretary to Ivo de Tailboys, Baron of Kendal. 

He might have written Magna Charta, possibly having it dictated somewhere in his lord's manor to a group of clerks summoned for the purpose. We have no proof of this at all. Perhaps de Gilpin had nothing whatever to do with it. Since Langton was a powerful churchman and a principal instigator of the Baronial cause, it would seem likely that he would have been able to hand the work over to a nearby monastery. At the last minute twenty-five copies could be turned out at his command, provided there were a sufficient number of scriveners at hand, but without the illumination or the uniformity of lettering so lovingly worked over in the great religious works, for this was a rush order. It would certainly have been an easily available service to the prelate. Perhaps de Gilpin was a consultant, perhaps not; we are never told.

Although our history books say very little about Magna Charta as a piece of writing, it is worth considering. Let us look again at the parchment which hangs "brown, shriveled and torn in the British Museum," and think of the feverish fingers in the late spring of 1215 as they scratched their shorthand, "Johannes dei Gra Rex Angl Dos Hybrn Dux Norman Aquit, etc." Even the abbreviation marks are impatiently dashed in. They are omitted from the above because they are not easily reproduced in modern print. The phrase reads, of course, "Johannes dei Gratis, Rex Angliae, Dominus Hiberniae, Dux Normanniae et Aquitaniae," (John by the Grace of God, King of England, Lord of Ireland, Duke of Normandy and of Aquitaine) referring to the first English King to use the "Royal We," for up to the time of King John the King referred to himself in the singular, even in official documents. The more we scrutinize the actual writing, the more we may conjecture, and perhaps with a measure of validity.
