VIKING SHIP CHAPTER 265 The Vikings 

The great Age of the Vikings is usually set as beginning with the first recorded appearance of a Norse pirate fleet in A. D. 789, and the settlement of the Northmen in Normandy, according to the treaty of St. Claire-Sur-Epte in 911/12. Previous to that date large numbers of 

Northmen had been driven out of Ireland, and England had called an uneasy truce, by signing over a large portion of the Island to the invaders at the peace of Wedmore, in 878. This Viking Age occurred simultaneously with the migrations and subsequent wars throughout Northern Europe and Asia. Whether the wandering tribes were moved by over-population or over-grazing, it is hard to say, but when forces in what are now Russia and Mongolia pushed forward into Europe, the Scandinavians were forced to seek other homes. It was an Age of universal unrest, part of the same pattern which, many Centuries before, had led to the break-up of the Roman Empire. It was a prolonged period of movement and thrust, called by some scholars Folk- 

Wanderings. 

In 789, on the Dorset coast of England, three pirate ships landed, claiming to have come from Haerethland. The pirates killed the harbormaster, and sailed off with a load of plunder. Other such marauders appeared in 793 off Northumberland and attacked the 2457

Monastery of Lindisfarne. Jarrow was raided, Glamorganshire in 

Wales, the Islands of Man and Iona. After 802 the worst raids were largely confined to Ireland and the Western coasts of Islands of 

Scotland. 

Always there was a plan behind the invasions: First, periodic raids, then the capture of an island base or arsenal and, after ravaging the mainland, a final settling down and assimilation among the native peoples. After the Danes had settled in England, and after the peace of Wedmore, there were a few more raids, but such efforts were frustrated by King Alfred's ships. Then the Danes, under their two Kings, Godfred and Siegfried, laid waste the countries of the Rhinemouth and the lower Scheldt, and divided their forces. Some of them continued their destruction of Germany, and others ravaged Northern France. 

Then Normandy was settled, and in 1066 an army of assimilated Norsemen, imbued with the culture and religion of the Christian Franks, again entered and conquered England. 

Terrible were the raids of the Vikings. So fierce were they that the 

Church incorporated in the regular service the prayer: "From the fury of the Northmen, deliver us.” Yet when the Northmen actually settled in a land, they governed themselves in due accordance with a strict. code of laws, and it is said that the Viking raids were one of the determining causes of the establishment of Feudalism. Feudalism is often traced back to the custom of blood-brotherhood, shared by many of the Germanic tribes. Each chieftain, by this system, was a blood-brother and leader to his men, each of whom, in their turn, had sworn bloodbrotherhood to their fellows, for greater protection and group solidarity. If the Danes also practised the rites of blood-brotherhood, they too would have helped pave the way to the establishment of a system in which the leading Earls swore fealty to their King and, in turn, accepted the allegiance of other vassals.

As we progress in history we are justified in considering the expeditions of the Normans to be continuations of the sallies of the Northmen. The names are etymologically the same, and the people are also alike in descent. Both groups share in the old spirit of war and adventure, but the change of name signifies a deep change in historical position. The national character has suffered little change, but the Northern people have gained a new religion, a new language, a different code of laws, and a new social system. The effect of a settlement of Normans is vastly different from the effect of a settlement of Northmen. It is true that the Norse element in the Normans facilitated assimilation with people of an English and Danish back-

CHAPTER 265THE VIKINGS 

2459 ground, but they did not have a language closely related to English as did the Danes; and their institutions were completely foreign. Far from feeling a kinship with the Danes in England, the Normans found that the hard core of resistance was largely Danish. 

Somewhat later than the Danish conquests of England and Gaul came the Danish discovery and colonization of Greenland and Iceland. 

Eric the Red sailed from Iceland to Greenland in 985 and settled there. In 999 his son, Leif, set forth to the court of Olaf Tryggvason, King of Norway, and stopped on the way at the Hebrides. As he set out from Norway in 1000, the King commissioned him to proclaim Christianity in Greenland. On this voyage he was blown off course by bad weather and touched on the shores of North America, or Vinland, a land of which he had no knowledge. He took back with him "grapes," probably cranberries, the "selfsown" wheat which was, most likely, maize, and the bark and wood of the mösur, which scholars think was birch. These specimens he took back to his father's home in Brattahild or Ericsfiord, in Greenland. A later expedition is recorded in which 

Thorfinn Karlsefni came to the Western lands, accompanied by two Gaels, probably captured by Olaf Tryggvason. These men were swift runners, and were given to Leif because they had the makings of excellent scouts. Vinland was probably some part of Nova Scotia, perhaps seen by Biarni Haerilfson in 985. But Biarni never came ashore.

Thorfinn, allegedly followed upon his trail, exploring Helluland, Markland, and Vinland where he decided to spend a winter. 

Thorfinn was an explorer who went to Greenland and married there, his wife being the widow of Eric the Red's son Thorstein, named Gudrid. Thorfinn was greatly interested in founding a colony in Vinland. He took with him three ships, 160 men and some women, including Gudrid, and Freydis, Eric the Red's daughter.

Their route took them to Vesterbygd, or the "Western Settlement" of Greenland, Bear Island, and away to the South until they reached Helluland, probably Labrador, which took its name from the word Hellur, denoting slabs of rock. Two days later they reached the thickly forested Markland, meaning woodland, which might have been Newfoundland, and two days later they came to a cape where they found the remains of a ship, possibly the relic of an earlier Scandinavian explorer. The cape could have been Cape Breton or some nearby promontory, and its shores they called the wondrous beaches, "wonderstrands." After two days Thorfinn put his Gael runners ashore and told them to head Southward. When they returned they brought with them grapes and wild wheat, to show that they were near Vinland.

The fleet, now at anchor at Streamfiord, or the Firth of Currents, stayed for the winter (1003-1004) suffering Northern weather and hunger, and gaining no new knowledge of their Western promised land. In the Spring the mutinous Thorhall, Eric's huntsman, headed a band of nine men and sailed off to the North, with hope of working to the West and South, but bad weather drove them to Ireland and they were there enslaved. Thorfinn, meanwhile, forged Southward until he reached a place called Hop, at the mouth of a river flowing from a lake to the sea, which could have been one of the several estuaries near the Southernmost part of Nova Scotia. Here his group found wheat and vines enough to be assured that this was Vinland, and here they built their huts in 1004. Soon they were visited by natives, darkskinned, flat-faced, with high cheekbones, large-eyed and dark-eyed, with ugly hair, who approached them in skin canoes. The following

Spring brought the visitors back and Thorfinn and his company bartered with them. They were moved to panic by a bull belonging to the Northmen and returned in three weeks to fight. And so the 

Norse left Hop to the Eskimo, Heothuk, or Micmac Indians, whichever they were, and returned to Streamfiord. Thorfinn returned later to 

Hop for two months' visit, and then made a Northward trip in search of Thorhall. On this journey Thorwald Ericson was killed, apparently by a native arrow. Such are the stories told in the Red Eric Saga of three voyages, and in the elaborate account of six voyages in the 

Flatey Book. 

A discovery can be made but once, and it was Leif Ericson who, with the Northmen, discovered North America and attempted to colonize it. Leif was the first to be recorded as having come upon the 

Western Hemisphere. Three hundred years later Columbus arrived in the Carribean, heralding the movement of European expansion toward both the American continents. We cannot be sure of Red Eric's or Thorfinn's landings. They have been cited from Labrador to 

Florida. It has also been rumored that the Vikings at some time visited the shores of Massachusetts and Rhode Island. Had Iceland been close to European trade centers, the exploits of these Northern seafarers. would have had momentous consequences. As it was, they passed unnoticed.

In his article in the American Anthropologist, Arlington Mallery gives us the latest evidence to support the notion of Norse expeditions into territory now incorporated within the boundaries of the United States. The points he makes would seem to refute William Godfrey's statements of 1957, that there is no reason to believe that the Vikings

CHAPTER 265 – THE VIKINGS 

2461 were in any way responsible for the Newport Tower or were ever in that vicinity. Dr. Mallery shows that there was some evidence neglected by Godfrey when he claimed to have set down all theories pro and con, to that date, bearing on the pre-Columbian discovery of North 

America. Specifically, Dr. Mallery makes these three points: 

1) The only specific and irrefutable evidence of the Viking explorations of the North American coastline are the navigation charts with their Old Icelandic place names. Two of these, differing mainly in their zero points, are correct charts, and one, the Friseo Chart shows the coast of Maine and Nova Scotia. A third chart shows all of Canada 

East of Great Bear Lake and the Slave River, omitting Nova Scotia and a part of Ontario. It includes, however, the Northern areas of 

Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont and New York. In addition to the sixty or more ancient sagas which speak of North American explorations along the Northern shoreline made by the Vikings, these charts surely should convince us that such discoveries included a major part of Canada and certain portions of the United States and Alaska, several hundred years before the voyage of Columbus. 

2) There is some evidence of Viking contact with the North

American mainland in the longhouses of the Iroquois which so closely resemble the Norse longhouses. Indeed, some are almost identical to the narrow Scandinavian structures built prior to A. D. 1200. Where wood was not available the Scandinavian buildings were of stone. 

Only in the Iroquois' constant use of wood do we see a difference. And in these observations we learn that the Norsemen did build stone buildings, even though most of the old Scandinavian churches in the Old World are built of wood. This means that the Newport Tower could date back to Viking days.

A continuous line of longhouses was noted stretching between the Gulf of the St. Lawrence to Lake Huron. Recently a few more were discovered in Newfoundland, completing the chain of Viking houses, which after 1200 were built in a long chain from the Baltic Sea to Lake Huron. There are two types represented, reflecting the development of the Scandinavian skala and indicating two periods of Viking migration to America: a movement into the country South of the St. 

Lawrence River prior to 1200 and a period exemplifying a type evolved by the Iroquois descendants of the Vikings. The Iroquois, it would seem, continued building skala as late as 1800. Among the Neutrals (sic), an Iroquoian tribe, buildings are found bearing towers resembling the Scandinavian skemma.

3) In 1730 a mining surveyor employed by the Royal Board of Iron Trade of Great Britain went to Sweden to examine the Enkieling iron smelting furnaces then in use. His drawings (1734) show that four furnaces found in the Deer Creek Valley of Ohio in 1949 and 1950 and the older Scandinavian ones are identical (Lost America 

193c, 194a, 196aff, 216aff). It is obvious that the American Enkielings are of some antiquity, since they were completely buried within prehistoric Ohio mounds in areas previously undisturbed except by surface ploughing. Two iron shovels have also been found, one in an Enkieling furnace, and one in a hearth-pit furnace. It was found that the shovels had been made by cladding two carburized iron sheets together, the same process as that used in making a Viking axe excavated in Newfoundland.

Let us examine the evidence at Newport, Rhode Island, and see whether the stone Tower there could have been built by the Vikings. 

In Touro Park at Newport stands a squat, hollow Tower, a row of arches at its base, and an upper section missing. A picture made in 

1740 shows that there has been no change in its appearance to this date. Many would like to feel that it is an actual Viking monument, but the majority of archeologists who have investigated it insist that such a notion is untenable, that it is pure romance. In the Will of ex-Governor Benedict Arnold (grandfather of the Revolutionary Gen eral) dated 1677, there is mention of "My Stone Built Wind-Miln" which he bequeaths to his daughter. Those favoring a Colonial origin for the structure have gladly accepted this as a possible identification. 

However, the Will does not state that Arnold erected the Tower himself, nor do we know of a document that claims he did. There is no reason why he could not have used a tower already built as a basis for the wooden superstructure that would support the four sails. It would have saved him much labor if he had. There is no absolute proof of this "Arnold Theory." There are no Viking potsherds or any artifacts to be found at the Tower's base, nor is there any reason to believe that remnants have not been there. The earth around the 

Tower has been disturbed many times since Colonial days when, from time to time, legends of private treasure hoards have sent treasure hunters to the vicinity. It is also possible that some important clues have been destroyed by the shovels, picks, and crowbars of those who dug for gold. There is any amount of debris to be found, in such amounts that archeologists have felt that the Tower rested on a dumping ground, but that fact proves nothing. Thus far evidence of the 

Arnold theory has been negative, and such evidence tells us only that

CHAPTER 265 - THE VIKINGS 

2463 we still know nothing. Because the archeologists who believe that the 

Tower was a local product have proved nothing, the few definite facts supporting a medieval date seem, by contrast, impressive. The facts supporting a medieval origin are these: first, artifacts, found on allegedly undisturbed ground, have been unearthed near stones which have been pried loose. Many of these articles could have belonged to the treasure hunters. Most of the fragments of glass and pottery have been found concentrated in one small area. It would be unusual for builders to leave all their relics in a spot comprising only one percent of the whole area in which they worked, but a treasure hunter, prodding at the spot supposedly marked by X, would be the more plausible owner.

Even if the "finds" had been dropped by treasure seekers, we still have no proof that this is a Viking tower. But then, we have no proof that it was built by the earliest settlers. It might be well to examine the base structures of a few representative English and Dutch windmills and see if the tower is in any way like them. Let us then turn to the positive evidence for an earlier dating.

More dramatic is the story told by the measurements themselves. 

Whoever built the Newport Tower used a unit of length unknown to the English Colonists, a unit which had been abandoned several centuries before. It will be found that the tower is circular, and that the columns are equidistant from a common center, that their circumferences are precise circles with equal diameters. One would expect all the diameters to be given in whole numbers. Yet this is far from the case. The diameters of all circles in the plan are fractional, an unlikely way in which to lay out a building, particularly one designed with an eye to aesthetic appeal. One would expect a certain inexactness in measurements used with rough stones, and an error of an inch or two would raise no criticism. An error of nine inches, however, in a distance of less than twenty-five feet is unbelievable. Measurements of the various diameters have been checked and rechecked, but do what we will, they are still capricious, and a different system of measurement tallies with the measurements of the Tower. 

Obviously a measure different from the modern foot or yard was used. Our present yard varies about a hundredth of an inch from that used in 1490, in the reign of Henry VII, and another in 1588, in Elizabeth's time. This was the measure employed by our first settlers and nothing like the unit which is used as a base for the dimensions in the Tower. There was a common foot unit, in use in the Middle 

Ages and in Northern Europe, which was the Rhenish-Danish-Nor-

wegian foot of 0.3139 meters or 12.35 English and American inches. 

And it is this foot which was used by the builders of the Newport Tower. Arithmetical experimentation shows that it is. Why should the early settlers use a measure differing from the common and legal measure in England? Could some of the Puritans have picked it up in Leyden? Why should they make their work difficult by using a foreign unit?

Another tangible bit of evidence is the remaining piece of a Catholic altar. There are grooves for a shelf along one wall. There seems to have been a table top attached to the wall, supported by corbels. The table top is 42 inches, not a suitable height for a household table and, under the top, about half way between the top and the ground, is a niche neatly finished, perfectly suited for the deposit of the Communion elements. It is not likely that a work bench would be fixed to the wall in the darkest portion of the room. The specifications for the structure exactly fit the description of an altar arranged for Catholic use. The aumbry beneath the top of the altar is quite usual. The blank wall could be used for a hanging or a crucifix, and the candles, at such a distance from the windows, would not be blown out. But there were no Catholics in the early years of the Newport 

Colony. In 1680 it was reported that none resided there. 

Prior to 1632, Sir Edwin Plowden and his associates petitioned King Charles I for a patent of land, with headquarters somewhere near the East end of Long Island. In the petition is a list of existing resources within that tract of land and among them is named a large round stone tower. The tower was not on Long Island, and seems to have been at some distance on the mainland. How likely is it that there would have been two such towers? Has anyone found the foundation of so sturdy a building anywhere in that area? Something would have been left, overgrown and buried. No ploughshares have crumpled in the contact with a mysterious circular foundation. It is almost certainly the Newport Tower which is referred to, a facility which had been reported but not explained by someone who noted it earlier. 

The petition was granted in 1632, nearly seven years before the first settlers came to Newport.

Perhaps these statements do not seem entirely convincing. Nevertheless, there seem to be possible grounds for supposing that there was a tower on the Newport site when the English Colonists first arrived, and that it was built in the medieval period. Hjalmar R. Holand attaches a photograph to his article of the Abbey of St. Bavo in Ghent, Belgium. The tower beside the cloister looks almost exactly like the

For what purpose was the Tower built? In his poem, "The

It is commonly felt that Longfellow was alluding to the Newport Tower in the lines quoted above. We cannot truly believe that it was used as a private home as he does, nor does the altar mean that the tower was necessarily part of a church or monastery. It would be more in the fashion of the Celts to found monastic institutions on a voyage, or to make a voyage to seek out some lonely promontory for a monastery. 

The structure would be, most likely, a fort, possibly a stronghold against the Indians. By 999 the Norsemen were Christian, and some remnant of the "Age of Faith" would have touched them. Mass would have been sung by candle light in the stone chamber, as a prelude to a foraging expedition or an exploratory voyage or, for that matter, to herald every dawning day.

If indeed the Danes were responsible for the Tower, which stage of their development would it represent? From the preceding paragraphs, it would seem most likely that the style of architecture is intended to be Norman.

Romanesque is the name given to the style of architecture prevalent in Europe between the time of Constantine the Great, A. D. 325 and the year 1000. The name is also applied to a span of time, the 

Romanesque period. The Viking voyages certainly fall within that span, occurring as they do between 999 and 1003, encompassing the last five or more years of that period. Norman architecture is Romanesque, further developed. In France there was a richer treatment of detail. In England Norman architecture is sometimes called English 

Romanesque. The Newport Tower bears characteristics of both styles. 

The Viking explorations were not too early for Viking knowledge of Romanesque construction. If, as Dr. Mallery says, the units of measure used is a Church unit, the design may have been dictated by Norse churchmen travelling with the expeditions.

Three times the Danes played an important part in the history of a nation which became the world's greatest Naval Empire. In the days of the early Germanic invasions, a poem was carried to Britain from some area on the banks of the Vistula. It told of those who called themselves the Spear-Danes and, beneath a thin veneer of Christian coloring, we read the primitive take of how the Spear-Danes, in days gone by, called upon a Goth warrior to help them destroy a brace of monsters who were killing off the heroes who attended King Hrothgar and Queen Waeltheow at Heorot. The manuscript is dated after 

A. D. 700, but was written before the Angles, Saxons and Jutes established themselves in England. As in the Sagas, we hear in these early poems of the life of the wanderer and the seafarer, or "wolf," whose days are filled with wind, ice, storm and spray. He urges his rowers down the "whale's way," the ocean, in a "Dragon" ship, and comes to the shore of England, versed in the use of the "blood-drinker,” or sword, laden with heavy gold arm rings to be used as currency. The 

Britons were defeated, driven back to the Welsh marches and the Scottish hills, and a state evolved, a highly organized state with a strictly formulated code of laws, with councils and varying ranks of government officials. In time Alfred became King. Religion, history, local tradition and philosophy were translated by monks, according to his decree into the Anglo-Saxon language. A later surge of Nordic seafarers then came to England, to attack, conquer and settle down in the Northern portion of the Island. They cost Alfred much hardship and many men. This was between the years 800 and 900. Then 166 years later, a band of French-speaking Christians, Vikings some generations before, conquered England, already twice claimed by Scandinavians.

These facts give us some clue to our conclusions concerning the Tower. We can only say that the evidence published in 1951 gives us an adequate basis for belief in a medieval origin. But we cannot be more specific. We still have no proof that the Vikings built the Tower. 

It is probable, however, that it was built by Europeans at a date later than 1000, if the similarity to the Belgian Abbey is trustworthy. There have been theories about an exploration in 1380 or thereabouts. The explorers of that period were supposed to have been monks who left their island monastery near Scotland and sighted the coast of Cape Breton. But this is just another romance. There is not an iota of proof. Yet it seems likely that the Tower had been built by persons more interested in a permanent foot-hold than the semi-foraging Danes. 

And if the Danes had built a watchtower to command the shore line,

CHAPTER 265 - THE VIKINGS

ROBIN HOOD THE ARCHER CHAPTER 266 

Robin Hood of Sherwood Forest

There are few who have not heard of Maid Marian, of Robin Hood, or of his foresters, the doughty archers who wore the Lincoln green and who lived in the good Greenwood of Sherwood Forest: 

Alan-a-Dale, Midge, Will Stutely, the foppish Will Scarlet and the burly Little John, who cudgeled Robin Hood on the bridge. To these the Geste adds Gilbert of the White Hand and Reynold. 

The question is, how much of this pleasant lore belongs to history and how much to legend. The various characters in the cast may have been added to Robin Hood's company at different times, and it is also possible that when the Robin Hood tradition absorbed them they had come into the story fully accoutered with traditions of their own. 

Will Stutely is a late addition, we know, and he became so popular in the 16th Century that a pedigree was drawn up for him, though his place in history was more shadowy that that of Robin Hood himself. 

Robin Hood has been described as "the hero of a group of old English ballads, represented as an outlaw and a robber, but of a gallant and generous nature, whose familiar haunts are the Forests of Sherwood and Barnsdale, where he fleets the time carelessly in the merry Greenwood. He is ever genial and good natured, religious, respectful to the Virgin and to all women for her sake, with a kind of gracious and noble dignity in his bearing. He lives by the king's deer, though personally most loyal, and wages ceaseless warfare on all proud bishops, abbots and knights, taking of their superfluity and 2474

CHAPTER 266 — 2475 

ROBIN HOOD 

giving liberally to the poor and to all honest men in distress, of whatever degree. He is unrivaled with the bow and quarterstaff; but in as many as eight of the extant ballads comes off the worse in the combat with some stout fellow, whom he thereupon induces to join his company."

A stalwart curtail friar called Friar Tuck in the title, though not in the ballad, fights with Robin Hood, and apparently accepts the invitation to join his company, as he appears later in two broadsides which also mention Maid Marian. Such in the romantic figure of the greatest of English popular heroes, a kind of yeoman counterpart to the knightly Arthur, who is the hero of Tennyson.

Robin Hood is first mentioned in the second edition of the B text of Piers Plowman, a long poem of social protest, which has been dated 

1377. Here, a character called Sloth says: "I know not my Pater Noster perfectly as the priest singeth,

But I know rhymes of Robin Hood, and Randolf, erle of Chestre." 

The language of Piers Plowman is a middle English which may be laborious to read. The above is a modified version. The ballad of 

Robin Hood and the Monk very possibly dates as far back as the reign of King Edward II. Robin Hood and the Potter and Robyn and

Gandelyn are of 15th Century date at the latest. A Lytle Geste of 

Robyn Hode (Geste meaning a"song of deeds" as in chanson de geste) was printed by Wynkyn de Worde in 1510, but it could have been written in the 15th Century, and there is little doubt that the separate ballads from which it was composed are of a still earlier date. The 

Scottish historian Fordun wrote of Robin Hood in 1386; so it would seem that the Robin Hood tales had reached a peak of popularity in the mid-14th Century, and maintained their popularity through the reign of Elizabeth and well on through the reign of King James. 

One man sometimes mentioned as the historical Robin Hood is ROBERT FITZ OOTH. He is said to have been an outlaw nobleman who became the lover of Matilda, the daughter of Robert FitzWalter, the Surety. The only possible explanation for a name like Fitz Ooth is that it is a transformation by folk etymology from Fitz Otho. There was a Fitz Otho in history, an early lord of Windsor Castle, Walter Fitz Otho or Fitz Other, appointed in 1078 by William the Conqueror as Warden of the forests of Berkshire. He had a son Robert, a younger son, who could not have used the paternal given name as a last name, nor could he have used it in the combined form, FitzWalter-Fitz Otho. 

Yet his connection with forests, as son of a "minister of forestry," and a misappropriation of the name FitzWalter, associating him in the

popular mind with the woodland swain who saved the daughter of the later FitzWalter of Dunmow Castle from the frustrate savagery of King John, probably brought him into the Robin Hood legend in the 14th Century, or at least brought a shadow of him into it. But everything was distorted when his memory was added to the Robin Hood tradition, even his father's name Otho (Otto). 

Robert was the Baron of Eston or Estaines of co. Essex in the historical account, and his son William had a daughter who married 

Robert de Hastings. They had a daughter, Delicia, who married 

Henry de Cornhill, and their daughter Jane married Godfrey de Lovaine. Matthew de Lovaine, son of Godfrey, had a daughter who married into the Bourchier family, and they kept the Eston holdings until the time of King Henry VIII. 

Robin Hood's identity will always remain clouded. He doubtless was an historical character, probably a local outlaw and small poacher whose story had become romanticized, thereby creating an appeal to those of the surrounding communities. As the tradition grew it absorbed the French pastoral songs and stories of the country boy and girl, Robin and Marian, who are to be found immortalized in Adam de la Hale's opera of the early 13th Century. The French country heroine becomes merged with the Maid Marian of the May dances and subsequent association with rural games, tattered remnants of earlier fertility cults.

The tale of Robin Hood gathered up fragments of popular romances, such as The Foure Sonnes of Aymon, a romance so popular that William Caxton felt called upon to print it and make it available to a wider audience. It ranks with England's first printed books and 

England's best sellers. The romance of Gamelon, the forerunner of 

Shakespeare's As You Like It, was also woven into the Robin Hood web. Again it is a tale of rebels forced to flee the law and live in the forest. In the Shakespeare play the foresters are noblemen gone wrong.

The tradition may also have absorbed the peasant trend preserved in the Flemish beast tale of the rogue hero, Reynard the Fox, who is ever at variance with the robber Baron, Isengrim the Wolf, and with the Church; for his disguise as a friar, like Robin Hood's, is considered a fitting rebuke to the corrupt clergy.

As the Robin Hood tradition progresses it degenerates, as did the Arthurian tales and ballads. No longer is the notion of simple piety and chivalry palatable. It has been reiterated much too often. The stories of Sir Gawain have become the stories of a prig, and the hero is set up for ridicule. Likewise Robin Hood becomes a figure of fun,

CHAPTER 266 – ROBIN HOOD 

2477 and the later ballads are doggerel, dealing with buffoonery and vulgar practical joking, allying the tradition at least in spirit with the tales of Reynard.

Some have said that Robin Hood was a Saxon of the 12th Century, still holding out against the Norman occupation, or a symbol of that stubborn, taciturn resistance; and some have said that he and Little 

John were two heroes who were with Simon de Montfort at the Battle of Evesham, though we have no guide as to what led anyone to this supposition.

Simon de Montfort, Earl of Leicester, was fighting against the forces of young Prince Edward. The Prince managed to defeat Leicester in the Valleys of the Severn and the Usk. They approached Evesham on 4 August 1265, in time to cut Leicester off from Kenilworth Castle, where the forces of the younger Montfort had already been cut to pieces. The Earl found himself caught in the bend of the River Avon, blocked by the ranks of the Royalist forces. With near superhuman savagry he cut his way out, and chopped his path Northward. But now as success seemed almost a certainty, his Welsh levies drifted away and defeat was soon inevitable. On Green Hill, to the Northwest of the town of Evesham, his devoted followers formed a ring around their lord and died with him in combat. Were Robin Hood and Little John there? It seems doubtful.

Robin Hood has also been associated with a rebel Earl of Lancaster in the reign of Edward II. The most rebellious Earl of that reign was Thomas, the son of Edmund, surnamed Crouchback who, tired of the feckless and psychotic Monarch and his worthless, pleasureloving favorites, the younger Hugh Despencer and Piers Gaveston, rebelled and was beheaded for treason at Pontefract. Crouchback was created Earl of Lancaster in 1267 and his son Thomas would have been too late for the Robin Hood role, for the legend was complete by the mid-14th Century. For the same reason, it would seem unlikely that the forester was one of de Montfort's men. 

There are indications that Robin Hood has been identified with Robert Locksley, a murderer of Bradford in Hallamshire, and that he was Robert FitzOoth, Earl of Huntington. The latter tradition seems to have derived from a play of 1598 called the Downfall. In it Matilda, daughter of Robert FitzWalter, Baron of Bayard and Dunmow, and

the Leader of the Magna Charta Barons, was importuned by King John. She thwarted her royal lover by eloping with Robert FitzOoth and fleeing with him to Sherwood Forest. There, according to one version, the two bided virtuously apart until a marriage could be conveniently arranged. Another version has it that Friar Tuck was ready to receive them in an appointed glade, where he married them. 

It is certainly true that there were tales of King John's attempt to seduce Baron FitzWalter's daughter, or any Baron's lady within reach of the Court. In the Historie des Ducs de Normandie (p. 118) it is mentioned specifically as a tale told to King Philip. The Chronicle of 

Dunmow Abbey printed in the Monasticum (Dugdale, Monasticum 

VI, 147) says that the King when frustrated attempted to poison

Matilda. This story, and that other of John's attempted rape on the person of the wife of the Surety Eustace de Vesci, seem to be backstair gossip, refurbished in order to show why these two lords rebelled against their King, and also to serve generally as propaganda, though it would seem that the truth alone could condemn King John sufficiently. Still, the elopement of Matilda and Earl FitzOoth has no substance.

A freer version of the above has it that Robin Hood was Robert 

FitzOoth, Earl of Huntington in Locksley, Nottinghamshire. Once again we hear the name Locksley. The other time it was the outlaw's surname. Such are the ways of oral tradition. He is said to have contracted a fever and to have gone to his kinswoman, the prioress of the nunnery of Kirkless, for aid. She thereupon cut the appropriate vein for the medication of bleeding and did nothing further. Robin subsequently bled to death. The date of the episode is definitely set as 

18 November 1247. 

The phrase concerning Robin Hood in Piers Plowman does not assert that he was Randolf, Earl of Chester. Sloth merely says that he knows rhymes of Robin Hood and of the Earl of Chester. This linkage, however, has caused some to believe that Robin Hood and the Earl of 

Chester were one.

Ralph, Ranulph, Randle, or Randolph de Blundvill (ca. 11721232) succeeded Hugh de Keveliok as Earl of Chester in 1181. He was created Earl of Lincoln in 1217. He married Constance, the widow of 

Geoffrey of Brittany, son of King Henry II. He fought for King John in Wales against the Barons in the dispute over Magna Charta, and was an Executor for the King. He was in the army of King Henry III, fighting against the French invaders and their allies. In 1218 he went on a Crusade and took part in the siege of Damietta. He returned home

CHAPTER 266ROBIN HOOD 

2479 to England and died in October 1232 at Wallingford. Stubbs says of him, "On more than one occasion he refused his consent to taxation, which he declared unjust; his jealousy of Hubert de Burgh, although it led him to join the foreign party in 1223, did not prevent him from more than once interposing to prevent his overthrow." Randolph's unique position in the kingdom "fitted him for the part of leader of the opposition to royal or ministerial tyranny." Was this Robin Hood?

The date is better suited for the start of the legend. But this was a man of arms and armies, a fully caparisoned lord who supported his king, fought openly in the field of battle, and wore the Crusader's Cross. We cannot possibly imagine him defying in any way the organized power of the Church, let alone skulking about in the woods or having any part in guerilla warfare. 

If Robin Hood were not the lover of Matilda, the widow of Theobald Walter, perhaps he had some connection with Fulke FitzWarin. 

Fulke's story is told in a romance. The connection again is probably an accretion of details, taken from Fulke's story, associated with other popular romances of outlaw heroes. 

The romance Fouke FitzWarin is the tale of an historical person. 

He was a simple knight of minimal landed power. He defied King 

John, urging his friends to revolt, and went into hiding for three years with a band of outlaws. They did not, however, stay in any one place, nor did they live solely in the forest as archers. Their exploits were on both sea and land.

Fulke FitzWarin was later pardoned at the request of two of the King's most intimate friends, and he was given those things which he had originally sought. Finally he was granted the hand of a rich widow in marriage. Perhaps the story is true, odd as it sounds. John might have felt that a man who could defy his government successfully for three years was too good a man to lose. Soldiers were a valuable asset to a feudal monarch and, doubtless, fighting men of Fulke's calibre were not often found. Fulke seems to have been active in Shropshire in 1200 and 1201. On 30 April 1202 we have a record of the King's pardon of one Eustace de Kivelly who had incurred outlawry by being a companion of Fulke.

Again we ask, was Fulke FitzWarin Robin Hood? The story does not suggest it any more than does Randolph's. The dates of both are the earliest we have for possible historical heroes who might have given rise to the Robin Hood legend. No one has yet proposed a candidate dating to a time before 1200.

ROBIN HOOD THE DEFENDER 

Robin Hood could have been a recognized historical hero but, if he were, the historical personage has become so obscured by the various accretions that he is now entirely unrecognizable. Since the legend was popular in the mid-14th Century, it would have taken some time to build up, and it would seem likely that its roots are to be found at the latest in the first years of the 12th Century. However, there is no reason that the original man should not have dated back to a much earlier time. We have found that it is fairly easy for an historical person to become the focal point of a legend or even a myth. In our own background we have tales of thunder caused by Hendrik Hudson and his crew bowling in the Catskills, and of its origin in the cannon of the "Bonhomme Richard" as she sails the stormy seas. Surely Robin 

Hood is more likely to be a human being than these demigods. Whoever he was, he has become hopelessly confused with other persons of historical and legendary note.

A ballad about a local lad who ran with a rural gang would, on the other hand, have been quite sufficient to make the beginnings of a Robin Hood romance: A story of a young leader who lived on the 

King's deer and gave the spoils of his larceny to beggars. Couple that with peasant resentment of the ferocious taxes of King John's reign, the tradition of cruelty connected with the feudal nobility, and middle class distrust of high ranking Church officials, and the rest comes naturally. The legend appealed to the lower classes, as the Arthurian romances appealed to the aristocracy. There was no yeoman who was deaf to the call, "Come hither, come hither, come hither. No enemy shall he see, but winter and rough weather." And every knave who

CHAPTER 266 - ROBIN HOOD 

2481 was wont to "tune his merry note unto the sweet bird's throat" knew the boyish delight of poaching and tried his prowess with the long yew bow. It does not, in the final analysis, seem necessary to suppose that the historical Robin Hood was an historical celebrity. He probably was some one, we know not who, but perhaps a local rustic of Nottinghamshire or a neighboring shire. The date is probably the reign of 

King Richard I or King John. The sheriff of Nottingham, in some versions, is one of John's many tax collecting officials and the official devil and whipping boy. During John's reign the cost of court maintenance was high, and thus the prevalence of such persons as the famed sheriff, and stories of a series of attempts to outwit him would not be unlikely at that period.

Before we end our discussion of Robin Hood, let us give a thought to those of his company who have been discussed by scholars. Little 

John, the stout churl with the quarterstaff, was John Little or John Nailor. And it was a good joke to reverse his name, since he was a giant of a man. Friar Tuck, a fat but muscular Churchman, was apparently tolerated by Robin Hood. He was fond of showing that he was as brawny as any man in the Greenwood company. He was Chaplain to the little band and got his name from the fact that his habit was tucked or bloused over his cincture, to facilitate swift movement through the forest.

Maid Marian has been identified as Matilda, that sweetheart of the outlaw Earl, FitzOoth. She is, however, a later addition and is mentioned only after Robin Hood has become associated with the Mayday games and morris dances in which her role was played by a boy. She is represented with a wig of long hair surmounted by a golden crown and she carries a red carnation in her left hand. Friar 

Tuck is paired with her in the May game tradition. The association of Robin and Marian from the French tradition couples her with Robin Hood, whose costume of Lincoln green ties him in as a wood sprite and fertility deity, and he becomes her woodland lover and 

King of the May.

CHAPTER 267 

Rob Roy of the Highlands

The history of Rob Roy is bound up with the fortunes of Clan Gregor. Clan Gregor was a warlike faction that thought nothing of sweeping down from its Highland retreat and raiding nearby landholdings. About the year 1586 the Earl of Montrose felt the threat of the MacGregors of Glenstrae. In that year the Earl exacted a friendly "submission" from them, but he also had to invoke the law when they murdered Drummond, the King's forester of Glenartney. Poaching, robbery, strife and murder were a way of life for Clan Gregor. In 

1598 John Grant of Freuchie made use of a Charter granted him by the Earl of Moray over the lands and lordship of Abernethy, to take proceedings against the Gregor faction. His patience was exhausted and he finally executed two of them for theft in his Castle of Ballachastell and, in 1613, took prisoner Allister MacAllister, one of their ringleaders. Allister died while in Grant's custody, but apparently

Grant's actions against Clan Gregor were caused largely by Government pressure for, when that pressure was removed, it was found that he had actually given shelter to some of them. Thus it seems that as early as the last two decades of the 16th Century, the MacGregors were virtually outlaws, hunted out at the behest of the Government. 

Archibald Campbell, seventh Earl of Argyll (1575-1638) nicknamed "Gruamach" or "the Grim," was given a commission of justiciary against Clan Gregor on 1 February 1692/3. In 1592 he had narrowly escaped poisoning at the hands of one Campbell of Lochnell, a man closely connected with Clan Gregor, and next in line to the Earldom of Argyll. On 14 December 1598 he got another commission against the Clan, but his execution of it does credit neither to Argyll nor to the Government. The MacGregors had made a raid on Lennox and had killed eighty or more of the Colquhouns who had put up a severe resistance in Glen Fruin. Argyll was blamed for the bloodshed and was suspected of having let the massacre proceed as a means of ridding himself of his personal enemies, some of whom were Colquhouns. Pressure was brought to bear and Archibald the Grim plied the chieftain, Alexander MacGregor, with promises which, according to MacGregor's dying statement, were kept "only in the shadow, but broken in the substance." The outcome was the hanging of a Mac- 

Gregor Chief and seven of the Clan at Edinburgh, 20 January 1604.

Glen Fruin is one of the more famous glens in the Highland portion of Dumbartonshire. As was indicated above, the Colquhouns 2482

CHAPTER 267 — ROB ROY 

2483 were nearly exterminated in this Glen in 1603, and Clan Gregor was proscribed. That meant that they were henceforth to run wild through the raths and valleys, getting food where and how they could, and that the death of any one of them was sanctioned by the Government. 

It would seem that such measures would make worse criminals of them while they lived. This, then, is the family background of Robert 

MacGregor, better known as Rob Roy, or Robert the Red.

In 1662 the Scottish Parliament had completely outlawed the Clan, and it is at this later date that we meet Rob Roy, often under the name of Campbell, for he had assumed his mother's name as protection after the proscription had beeen officially announced. An early novel by Sir Walter Scott bears this hero's name as its title and, after indicating who and what he was, we might quote Scott's description of him.

In 1671 Rob Roy was born into the troublesome Clan Gregor. 

His outlaw life, however, had been ascribed to personal financial losses in 1712, which turned him to a life of robbery rather than to the Government proscription on his Clan, dating back some sixty years or more before his birth. His legend is localized in the vicinity of Loch Katrine and Loch Lomond, consisting of romantic escapes. from prison, evasions of pursuers, plunder of the rich and generosity to the poor. He became the stock romantic bandit, a Highland Robin 

Hood. In some of these stories, folk who had benefited from his generosity warn him of his persecutors, the Duke of Athole and of course the Duke of Montrose, continuing the old border feud in the role of a Scottish sheriff of Nottingham. They tell of soldiery summoned by the aforesaid lairds from Dumbarton and Stirling, reminding us of the Western badmen, the posses of the law, ranch kings and wicked sheriffs of current romancing. 

The name of Argyll is still prominent in the story, but this time as an aid and protector, for Rob Roy had taken the name of Campbell, and the Campbells had long been the Earls of Argyll. In his later years Rob Roy is said to have turned to the Roman Catholic Church, but in the list of subscribers to the Episcopalean Church History of 

Bishop Keith we find the name of "Robert MacGregor alias Rob Roy."

Since the Church of England was the most likely non-Roman Church with an Episcopal organization, barring Methodism, it might seem that Rob Roy was possibly being politically unwise in his choice of a religious faith, for it was in his Century that Prince Charlie had plans for relieving King George III of his Crown. But Rob was both a natural rebel and a declared criminal, and treason or treacherous acts might be normal for him.

Rob Roy died in his own home at Balquhidder 28 December 1734, apparently of natural causes. He had five sons, two of whom died in the same year as their father. James and Robin paid with their lives. for their crimes-James as an outlaw in Paris and Robin on the gallows at Edinburgh for abduction.

Sir Walter Scott describes Rob Roy as "rather beneath the middle size than above it; his limbs were formed upon the very strongest model that is consistent with agility. Two points in his person interfered with the rules of symmetry: His shoulders were so broad . . . as to give him the air of being too square in respect to his stature; and his arms, though round, sinewy and strong, were so very long as to be rather a deformity." (Rob Roy MacGregor xxiiii)

It is interesting to note that another MacGregor has perpetuated the name of Rob Roy. This was the son of General Sir Duncan Mac- 

Gregor, K. C. B., canoeist, traveler and philanthropist. John Mac 

Gregor (1825-1892) had a roving disposition, a love for mechanics as well as for literature. He traveled through Europe, Egypt, Palestine, Russia, Algeria and America, while pursuing his researches in the history and methods of marine propulsion. He is considered the pioneer of British canoeing. In 1865 he made famous his canoe, Rob Roy with his tour of the waterways of Europe. His book, A Thousand Miles in the Rob Roy Canoe made his journeys and his craft one more factor in the MacGregor romance. Many longer trips were to follow and to be written up. Thus a MacGregor again made the name of Rob Roy famous for romantic vagabondage and adventure.

CHAPTER 268 Madoc of Gwynedd 

Another hero half historical and half legendary is Madoc, the pre-Columbian visitor to our Southern shores. According to Welsh tradition he was the son of Owen Gwynedd (Gwyneth), King of North Wales, who died in 1169. Madoc is said to have set sail in 1170 and to have established a colony on the Southern branches of the Missouri. 

He returned to Wales and brought more companions with him to North America. There is some question as to how many voyages he made and whether or not he was on the final one, which never returned to Wales. Concurrent with Madoc's voyages was the desertion of Aztlan by the Aztecs, who chose as their leader Yuhidthiton and with him founded the Empire of Mexico and named their nation for Mexitli, their tutelary god. Robert Southey's epic, Madoc, written about 1810, combines these two traditions. 

There has been much discussion of Madoc and Mexico. According to Southey, Madoc lived there many years. Some legends tell how he became a culture-hero god, the white god who came from nowhere and spread new knowledge among the people, only to return to the place of his mysterious origin, with a promise to return. He has often been identified with Quetzlcoatl. One reason for this supposition is that Quetzlcoatl means "winged serpent." The frequent carvings of winged serpents found in the ruins of Aztec buildings are his symbols. 

Some people have supposed that this winged serpent was suggested by the griffin or dragon on Madoc's signet ring for, as a member of the Welsh royal family, he would surely bear the red griffin of Wales; and a winged serpent, authority and godhead would have been considered identical by the Aztecs. Apparently Quetzlcoatl was of a light complexion, or white. Seemingly he was bearded. A beard of any consequence is not to be found on an Indian face. He does not seem to have been of the same racial stock as his followers, but is that any proof that of all white men he was Madoc?

Let us now go back to Wales and see how that Country was faring for some two hundred years before Madoc's birth. Before the reign of 

Stephen it had been well under English control, but the Welsh saw hope for independence during the chaos of King Stephen's regime, and sought to take advantage of the preoccupation of the English with their own confused affairs. Owen, son of Griffith ap Cynan, heir to the throne of Gwynedd, and Griffith ap Rhys, ruler of Dynavor, were strong men and gave courage to the Cymry. In 1136 Griffith ap Rhys met a large English contingent near Cardigan, a contingent composed of the 2486

CHAPTER 268 – MADOC 

2487 combined forces from the castles of South Wales and bands of the hated Flemish colonists which King Henry II had planted in Dyfed. 

A fierce battle ensued in which the Norman-Flemish forces were driven back. The following year, 1137, the two above mentioned princes died -Griffith ap Cynan, "the sovereign and protector and peacemaker of all Wales," and Griffith ap Rhys, "the light and strength and gentleness of the men of the South."

In 1157 King Henry II made an expedition into North Wales and forced Owen, son of Griffith ap Cynan, to become his vassal. This achievement was brought about by arms, and the English onslaughts were met by an army of offense, which more than once caused the English army to retreat. Finally, an insecure peace was made. In 1169 

Owen Gwynedd died. He was buried at Bangor Cathedral, after a reign of thirty-three years in which he was partly successful in bringing about a union of all Wales, a union which his grandson was to complete. 

According to the Caradoc History of Cambria [See H. Lloyd, The

Historie of Cambriae now called Wales... New Created, Augmented and Continued out of Records and Best approved Authors (David 

Powell, 1584)] Owen's rightful successor was Iowerth Drwynden, known as Edward of the Broken Nose. Being so self-conscious about this mutilation that he considered himself unfit to take upon himself the government of his Country, his younger brothers had visions of attaining the throne. Howell, a half-brother, however, soon took advantage of the bickering among his brothers, and planted himself on the throne, whereupon the other half-brother, David, devoted his energies to getting him off. This was no easy task, for what Howell had taken, Howell was going to keep. In the end, David and Howell settled the matter in a duel. Howell was killed, and David was unanimously proclaimed Prince of North Wales, enjoying that title until his nephew, Llewelyn ap Iowerth, (not Llewelyn the Great, also a 

Llewelyn ap Iowerth) came of age. 

Is it surprising then that the youngest of Owen's sons should take to the sea? Furthermore, David married Emma, King Henry II's half sister. This action discomfited the Welsh people, who felt that such an alliance could only lead to a betrayal into the hands of their ancient enemy. Their fears were justified when David, soon after his marriage, sent a thousand men to serve under King Henry in Normandy. Later 

David went to Oxford and entered Parliament, swearing allegiance to the King of England. This rebirth of international ill will seemed to be another annoyance to the introverted Madoc, causing him to seek peace on the high seas.

Before we go further, let us look at a plan of Madoc's family and lineage. 

Maelgan Gwynedd, King of Wales, fl. 350. 

Llewellyn ap Seissgylt, died 1022, married Angharad. 

Griffith ap Cynan, King of Gwynedd, died 1137. His son Owen ap Griffith, died 1169, married first Brenda, daughter of Howell,

Lord of Caro, and had: Cynan, who had Rhun, who had Iowerth, who married and had Llewlyn, who later threatened David's title to the throne. He had Maelgan, who had Rhodi, who had Rhiryd (Eiryd), Lord of Colochran, Ireland, and was the father of Madoc. 

Owen ap Griffith married second Christiant and had David, who married Emma, half sister of King Henry II.

Madoc, son of Owen and Brenda, above, married Annesta, Christiant's maid of honor, and had Gwenllian, who married

Llowerch ap Bran, descended from Rhodri Mawr (Roderick the Great) the greatest of the Welsh kings and, according to legend, of Arthur's blood. 

Owen ap Griffith married third Pyog, a lady of Ireland, and had Howell.

The tradition is that Madoc established a colony in North America and that his companions intermarried among the Indians. A letter written in 1782 by John Sevier, Governor of Tennessee, quotes statements made by the Cherokee chieftain, Oconostota, who said that there were in Tennessee white men who were Welsh, and who had come over a Great Water. They had landed, he said, at the Bay of 

Mobile. "I asked him," wrote Sevier, "if he had heard his ancestors say what nation of people these whites belonged to. He answered he had heard his father and grandfathers say they were called Welsh; that they had crossed the Great Water and first landed near Mobile and had been driven up the heads of the waters until they had arrived at the Highwassae River," which is not far from Chattanooga. 

According to the accounts in Caradoc and Hackluyt, Madoc returned to Wales, overbrimming with joy over his new discovery and eager to tell his countrymen all about the new land. He had left one hundred twenty Welshmen on American soil, and was going back to invite others in Wales to share in his pleasure in the new land. The second expedition set sail, but when they landed not a trace could be found of the Welsh colony. Madoc searched in the South and West, and in so doing followed the shores of the Gulf of Mexico until he reached the mouth of the Mississippi at least, according to George Catlin.

CHAPTER 268 – MADOC 

2489 Apparently on his search he did not encounter the original pioneers who had been driven away from the coast by the Indians and had traveled North. Madoc, meanwhile, was heading toward Mexico where the adulation he received put his displaced countrymen completely out of mind. Some of them, it is said, set out to sea and, finding the Gulf Stream, sailed back to Wales.

A third expedition was organized and set forth. Since Madoc was not with them, we can only suppose that he had stayed in Mexico. 

The third group, so the legend goes, fared Southward and reached Florida. Others believe that it reached Guadaloupe, for Antonio de Herrara, the Spanish historian, says that Columbus found the remains of a European style of ship there, which he was unable to account for. We cannot, however, know much of this expedition, for the voyagers, once having embarked, were never seen again. 

Some early travelers have testified that they had encountered Indians who could understand Welsh, though little is mentioned about their speaking it. These Indians were white, and they were bearded. 

They also owned skin covered books or parchments which they held in high esteem but which they could not read; but then practically no 

European out of Holy Orders could read. These books have been alluded to as "Bibles." There was, however, no Welsh translation of the 

Bible and printing was not accomplished until 1172. The Bibles were probably small psalters, handwritten in Latin, which had been brought by priests, and which had come into the hands of the Indians when the priests had died. No expedition of the 12th Century would have ventured forth without a priest, and no priest would have gone anywhere without a psalter.

The remarks made about the Indians who understood Welsh are interesting. Understanding a language differs from speaking it. Emotion can sometimes be communicated even when the gestures and facial expressions of another culture convey no meaning. It is said that the Indians knew what was going on at dramatic moments, that they knew that a Welshman, condemned to death, was praying. Are not the intense emotions those most easily conveyed, and is it unusual for any human being to suspect that someone is reacting to a particular situation in a manner similar to that of almost anyone in his experience who had ever been faced with that situation?

The tradition of the Welsh or White Indians and the "Ten Lost Tribes of Israel" among the American Indians is of great interest. 

James Mooney in his Article in the American Anthropologist [IV (1891) 393-394] writes of the mixed descendants of Madoc's colony,

and traces the developments and elaborations of the tradition to an Article in the Turkish Spy, published in London about 1730. 

At first the Welsh Indians are described as speaking Welsh and references are made to Welsh Bibles, rosaries, crucifixes and the like, found in their possession. We find them near the Atlantic coast where they are first identified with the Tuscaroras of the Iroquois Tribe. By 

1776 they had retreated inland, to be found on the banks of the Missouri, North of St. Louis. A few years later they moved again, dwelling far up the Red River. They then went Westward and became identified with the Mandans, whose language seemed to Catlin to have a Welsh element. Then they became the Moqui, a Pueblo Tribe of Northeastern Arizona, and next the Modocs, whose name suggests Madoc. 

Their final appearance was in Southwestern Oregon before their disappearance in the broad wastes of the Pacific Ocean. See also H. W. 

Henshaw, "Popular Fallacies Respecting the Indians," American

Anthropologist [VII (1905) 104-113]. 

The Welsh Indian seems more and more improbable as one considers him, and Madoc's motive in leaving Wales is vague. Was he a coward, and if so, how did he manage to face the hardships of the voyage and the hard life in the wilderness? Perhaps he felt that the warfare at home was not worth his efforts, an emotion unworthy of a royal son. Possibly his courage was suited to one sort of danger and not to another. However it may have been, Richard Hackluyt's 

Principal Navigations, printed in 1589, and his Discourse on Western

Planting, printed in 1600, helped Great Britain to assert her claim to America, largely on the strength of the Welsh discovery and settlement of that Country. "It is much more improbable that there should be no foundation for the reports that have been made since Madoc's voyages," claims George Burder, "and the instance of the Welsh Indians in North America, than that an expedition should have been undertaken in the 11th Century, similar to those which were frequently performed in the 15th. The mariner's compass was probably known at the former period, for it is described by a French poet who wrote early in the 13th Century, but the application of astronomy, which had been customary from remote antiquity, might have sufficed for a voyage to America with persons who had courage enough for the enterprise. Britain was at the time celebrated for its Marine and indeed had been for six hundred years."

Burder's book, The Welsh Discovered America, was printed in London in 1797. At that time the idea of the Noble Savage was still

CHAPTER 268 - MADOC 

2491 a prevalent sentimental myth, and it is all too likely that since most of Madoc's followers never returned, they were thought to have met sympathetic and noble souls among the savages, or that they had attained a blissful life in "Virginia" with feathered persons of great courtesy. Exactly what part the Noble Savage element has played in building up this tradition we cannot say, but the fact that the greatest amount of discussion of the Indians and the Welsh was written in the late 18th Century, coupled with the belief of many people that the Indian's life was a desirable one (thanks of Rousseau) suggests some sort of interrelationship, perhaps a wishful thought, that the Welsh and the Indians really ought to have lived together. 

Contemporary anthropologists feel that the Madoc story is as purely legendary as the tales of Prester John. We cannot prove that any European was in the Alabama-Georgia-Tennessee area before 1540, the earliest date set for Spanish landings. Strange as it may seem, the 

Spaniards were persistently active even when the English had gained a foothold. The Spaniards were primarily interested in mining and maintained a good deal of secrecy about their mining operations. Consequently, they were working in the wilderness undetected by the English. Tales of white settlers who landed prior to the English were kept fresh in Indian lore by oral transmission. It is therefore quite possible that the reports relayed in the 18th Century of an earlier European landing were reports of Spanish foraging parties only two centuries earlier. Much can happen in two hundred years, much forgetting and embroidery. The tales of the Welsh in the Southeast are filled with the mention of mines. May they have been the hidden mines dug by the Spaniards?

2. JACOB ANDREW CARTWRIGHT, born in Davidson County, Tennessee, 

27 November 1844, was educated in private schools and later in the public schools when the latter were opened in Nashville in 1855, and was graduated from Yale University in the Class of 1867. He studied law in the office of his uncle, Judge 

Joseph Carter Stark, in Springfield, Tennessee, and began the practice of law soon thereafter in Nashville. He married 10 November 1881 Mary Hart, daughter of 

Henry Hart and his wife Huldah Hooper of Davidson County, descendants of pioneer Tennessee families. He served one term as County Attorney and had almost completed one term as Judge of the Second Circuit Court at the time of his death on 20 June 1909. He gave of his time freely to civic, patriotic and religious activities. He served for several years as a member of the Nashville Board of Education, for a term was President of the Tennessee Sons of the American Revolution, was an Elder in the Cumberland Presbyterian Church and later in the Northern Presbyterian Church, when the two bodies merged. 

Judge Cartwright was a grandson of Jacob Cartwright and Patience Hobday his wife, and a great grandson of Robert Cartwright, formerly of Princess Anne County, Virginia, one of the first settlers on the Cumberland River in Middle Tennessee and a signer of the Cumberland compact of government on 1 May 1780. Through his father he was descended from the Shipp, Keeling, Lovett, Hunter, Johnson,

Langley, Thelabell and Mason families of Princess Anne County, Virginia. Six children: (a) Mary E. Pearson, d. 1936. 

(b) Lamiza A. Henderson. 

(c) Helen Grizzard. 

(d) Henry Hart Cartwright, d. 1933. 

1. (e) MARGARET CARTWRIGHT. 

(f) Jacob Andrew Cartwright, d. 1959.

This pedigree was made and set forthe, with much care and fidelity: Warrented by records, evidences and other good proofes, examined and approved, and well allowed by of by mee Sr Will'm Segar Kt al's Garter; and in assured testimony to all persons who shall see that it doth agree in all descentes Coates and Ensignes, and the registere, Bookes, and Recordes of my Office, and the Office of Armes and Hon'or kept at London, I the said Sr Will'm Segar al's Barter, Principall King of Armes have hereunto subscribed my name, & affixed the Seale of myne Office, this 

30th daye of Julye Ano D'ni 1630. Will'm Segar Garter.

*11. William Cole born 1598, died 1664, son of Humphreys Cole of Tillingham and his wife Hester, was born in England and died in Warwick County, Virginia. 

He came to Virginia in the Neptune, 1618, and settled in Elizabeth City County, where he received a grant of land in 1625. He was a member of the House of 

Burgesses in 1629, representing "Nutmeg" Quarter, a settlement which, in 1634, became Warwick City County. William Cole married Frances (maiden name unknown) and had a son William, born in 1638, and probably two other sons, John and Richard, mentioned at that period in Warwick County. *10. Honorable William Cole, born 1638, died 4 March 1694, established his home at "Boldrup," Warwick County, Virginia, pleasantly located on the Warwick River near Denbigh, and it was the seat of the Cole family for nearly a hundred years. 

Mentioned frequently as attorney in Warwick and York Counties and as Colonel of the military, he was named by Governor William Berkeley as a member of the Council in March 1675, serving continuously for seventeen years. During this period he was appointed by the King to be Secretary of the Colony, succeeding Nicholas Spencer 22 October 1689, and was a signatory to the petition to secure a grant from the Crown to build the college which became William and Mary. 

William Cole married first (name of wife unknown) by whom he had i.-Susannah. (1674-1708), who married Dudley Digges (1665-1710), son of Governor Edward

Mary College, 1723; Sheriff of Warwick County, 1726 and 1727; and elected a member of the House of Burgesses from 1718 to 1729. He married in 1710 Mary Roscow (1694-1750), daughter of William Roscow, Sr. (1664-1700) and his wife Mary Wilson (1675-1741), who was the daughter of Col William Wilson of Ceely's (1646-1713).

*1. (a) CLARENCE WALTER HILTON, born at Vorea, Orwell Township, Oswego County, New York, 8 December 1888, and married at Pulaski, New York, 8 December 1913, Mary Jane Clyde.

He received his education at the local schools and Central City Business 

School of Syracuse, New York. 

Mr. Hilton has been identified through the years with the building and contracting business. A dream was realized in the building of the 

Hilton Hotel at Syracuse, which he owned and operated for seventeen years. Among his other building projects are the Oswego County 

Tuberculosis Sanatorium; Onondaga Hospital, of which he was Chairman of the Board for fourteen years; a number of apartment houses and more than two hundred homes. 

Mr. Hilton was owner and operator of the Pulaski Natural Gas and Oil Company until its sale in 1932. 

His fraternal and club affiliations include: Central City Lodge No. 

305, F. and A. M.; Knight Templar; Shrine, and Jesters; Rotary Club;

Syracuse Lake Shore and Country Club; Skytop Country Club at 

Skytop, Pennsylvania; Miami Shores Country Club and Committee 

One Hundred at Miami Beach, Florida.

Mr. Hilton is also a member of the Sons of the American Revolution and a life member of the Somerset Chapter Magna Charta Barons.

Mr. Coling was graduated from the Buffalo University, College of 

Pharmacy. Mrs. Coling received her education at the local schools and the Onondaga General School of Nursing at Syracuse. Her fraternal and club affiliations include: Fralick Chapter No. 550, Order of the Eastern Star; Bethlehem Chapter No. 2, Order of the White Shrine of Jerusalem; Ildrim Temple No. 15, Daughters of the Nile;

Mrs. Coling is also a life member of The National Society Magna

Mrs. Coling had a son, John Albert Coling, born at Syracuse, New

*12. JAMES SHELTON I, Gentleman (son as above of Sir 

Ralph Shelton and his wife Jane West, eldest daughter of "the first

Lord De La Warre," perhaps William West, First Baron De La Warre, who died 30 December 1595) came with his uncle, Sir Thomas West

III, Baron de la Warra, Governor and Captain General of Virginia, 

(English records Stitch's and Smith's "History of Virginia," Alexander 

Brown's "Genesis of the United States," and "Record of the London

Company" by Kingsbury) to Virginia in 1610 and was a resident of 

Jamestown in 1620 (Smith, Volume 2, page 549).

James Shelton was a member of the Courts from 1619 to 1624 (Brown's "Genesis of the United States," "Records of the London Company"), and is given in the "Partial List of Families in America Entitled to Bear Arms" (William and Mary Quarterly, old series, Volume 1, Book 2, page 59). James Shelton was of Virginia and

Bermuda, where he died in 1668. His wife's name was Ann. Among other children they had

*11. Thomas Shelton, who owned large grants of land in Virginia and Maryland. He died in Cecil County, Maryland, where his Will was probated 4 May 1684, naming his son James Shelton as heir, without any mention of his wife, but an early deed refers to wife 

Hannah. They had 

10. James Shelton 2d, died about 1716, Clerk of York County

*9. John Shelton of "Currioman," Westmoreland County, Vir ginia, born 1649, died 1726, in 1670 built "Rural Plains" in Hanover

County, seven miles North of Richmond. The house today is in a splendid state of preservation and is considered to be the oldest house in America still occupied by a direct male descendant of the builder. 

In June 1957 Mrs. Crow had the honor of being the house guest of

*1. LUTEOLA GIBBS, born at Huntsville, Texas, 10 June 1878, where she married 18 November 1903 Henry Houston Warner Hawley, also of royal and baronial descent, born at Walla Walla, Washington, 6 January 1868, died at Dallas, Texas, 31 August 1937, son of Philip 

Livingston Hawley (and his wife Sarah Jane Roberts of Coshocton, Ohio) a descendant of Joseph Hawley I, of Stratford, Connecticut, and of Robert Livingston, First Lord of the Manor of Livingston,

Albany, New York, by grant of the King of England. 

Luteola Gibbs Hawley is a member of the First Methodist Church of Dallas. Her husband was a member of its Board of Stewards. After his death, it was decided to elect three women as Stewards, and his widow was among the number of women who first served the Church in that capacity. 

Mrs. Hawley is a Charter Member of the Dallas Bankers' Wives' 

Club; a member of the Dallas Woman's Club; the Craig Class Lecture 

Group; the Public Affairs Luncheon Club of Dallas; the Local History and Genealogical Society; the Dallas Southern Memorial Association;

Founder of the Southern Methodist University (an Alumna and a life member of the S. M. U. Mothers' Club); Kidd-Key College

Alumna; a member of the Kidd-Key Club and of the Randolph Macon 

Woman's College Alumnae Club. 

Mrs. Hawley is a Real Daughter of the Daughters of the Republic of Texas and a member of their State Officers' Club; Honorary Chapter 

Regent for life of the Daughters of the American Revolution, having served as DAR Chapter Regent, First Vice Regent and as DAR Chapter Registrar and Past State Treasurer. She is also Past President of the DAR State Officers' Club and Chapter Registrar for the United 

States Daughters of 1812. She served as State Secretary, State Regent, and is now Honorary State Regent of the Daughters of American Colonists and a member of the D.A.C. State Officers' Club. She is 

Past Vice President of the National Society of Daughters of American Colonists, being the first woman from Texas to be elected to a National Office by that organization; one of thirteen to be elected 

Honorary National Vice President for life, and is a member of their 

National Officers' Club (Past Director and Past Historian). 

Mrs. Hawley is also a member of the National Society of Colonial 

Dames of America Resident in the State of Texas, and a life member of The National Society Magna Charta Dames (Councillor for the 

Texas Division).

Children of Mr. and Mrs. Hawley: 

(a) Henry Houston Hawley, Jr., born at Huntsville, Texas, 14

July 1906, a graduate of Mrs. Taylor's School, of the Terrell

6. Heinrich Hefner, born about 1724, who came in the ship "Patience" from Rotterdam 19 September 1749, first settling at

Virginisville, Pennsylvania, where he was a weaver. He married 28

5. John Henry Hefner, born at Virginisville 23 November 1754, died 27 June 1825, married about 1777 Anna Catharine, born 26 

September 1759, daughter of John (and his wife Anna Maria) son of Beltzer Kohler of York County, Pennsylvania, a soldier in the 

War for Independence.

During the War he was a soldier in Captain Joseph Baldy's Company. In the winter of 1777-78 he with others were confined as prisoners in a church in New Jersey. One Christian Markel, also of Richmond 

Township, froze to death in Heinrich Hefner's arms. The following legal document is on record in the Court House of Berks County, Pennsylvania: "Berks County, ss: Whereas Heinrich Hefner, of Jacob Baldy's Co., in Col. Philip Gehr's Batallion, has made complaint to us, the 

Subscribers, Commissioners of said County, that he could not attend at Muster and Field days in 1777-78 as he was a prisoner of War and not exchanged, and we find his complaint just, do therefore, agreeable to an Act of General Assembly passed the 27th day of March, 1789, acquit and exhonerate the said Henry

*1. HONORABLE ROBERT ALEXANDER HEFNER, (c) 

above, was born near Lone Oak, Texas, 7 February 1874.

He worked

Li on his father's farm in Stephens County, Texas, until he was twentytwo years of age, without the privilege of attending either the grade or high schools. In 1899 he entered the University of Texas on a written examination and was graduated in 1902 with the degree of LL.B. On the recommendation of the Law faculty he was elected to a Fellowship in law in the University of Texas, where he taught law following his graduation. He practiced law in Ardmore, Oklahoma, from 1907 to 1926. Mr. Hefner was President of the Board of Education of Ardmore from 1910 to 1920; President of the Ardmore Chamber of Commerce; City Attorney, 1911-13; Mayor, 1919-27; President, Ardmore Rotary Club; Justice of the Supreme Court of Oklahoma, 192633; Deputy of the Grand Council of the Order of Demolay in 

Oklahoma, 1930; President of Patriotic Societies of Oklahoma, 195057. In 1949 he was elected a member of the Hall of Fame of the State of Oklahoma, and in 1950 a life member of the Board of Directors, Chamber of Commerce of Oklahoma City; Trustee, Oklahoma Baptist 

University; President, Dads' Association, University of Oklahoma, 1926-27; President, Oklahoma Memorial Association and of the State 

Municipal League of Oklahoma; Vice President, Navy League of the 

United States during World War II; Guardian of Scouting, Boy Scouts of America; Director, People's Building and Loan Association and 

Mid-Continental Life Insurance Company; member, Board of Directors, YMCA. 

Mr. Hefner is also a member of the Admirals' Club of New York 

City, Washington, D. C., and Fort Worth, Texas; of the American,

Oklahoma State and Oklahoma County Bar Associations; the American Judicature Society; Sons of the American Revolution; Oklahoma 

Historical Association (Director); Mason (K. T. Shriner) 32°; and a life member of The Plantagenet Society, the Somerset Chapter Magna Charta Barons and the Sovereign Colonial Society Americans of Royal Descent.

Judge Hefner voluntarily retired as Justice of the Supreme Court at the end of his term and resumed the private practice of law in Oklahoma City, in partnership with his son, Robert Alexander Hefner, Jr., under the firm name of Hefner & Hefner. In 1939 he was elected 

Mayor of Oklahoma City and served until 1947, at which time he voluntarily retired. Since then he has been engaged in the oil business with his two sons, Robert Alexander, Jr., and William J. Hefner. 

Mr. Hefner married at Jacksboro, Texas, 18 July 1906, Eva Johnson, PH.B., and L.M., North Texas Baptist College; A.B., Baylor Uni-
