William Hutchinson, born 1586, died 1642, son of Edward Hutchinson, who was buried at Alford 14 September 1631. They removed from 

Sandwich, co. Kent, to Massachusetts in 1634, where he was made 

Freeman the following year, and Representative to the General Court from 1635 to 1638, in which year they removed to Portsmouth, Rhode Island, where he was governor in 1639 and 1640. 

Mrs. Anne Hutchinson courageously lived up to her convictions. 

Being a Quakeress, she and her husband and fifteen children were banished from Massachusetts in 1638 and went to the Narragansett country where they purchased Aquidneck Island from the Indians and founded the town of Portsmouth, Rhode Island. After her husband's death she went "into the Dutch country west of New Haven" with John Throckmorton who, on 6 July 1643, obtained from Governor Kieft in New York for himself and thirty-five associates a grant of land in Westchester County, a point jutting far out into Long Island Sound. It is now called Throg's Neck (an abbreviation of the old spelling Throgmorton). We learn the settlement here was of short duration, as Mr. Winthrop records, in September 1643, that the Indians set upon the English who dwelt under the Dutch and killed "such of Mr. Throckmorton's and Mr. Cornhill's families as were at home." 

Anne Hutchinson and most of her young children were also among those cruelly murdered. However, issue survived through two sons and two daughters who escaped, the youngest of whom was 10. Bridget Hutchinson, whose Will was proved in 1698. She married first in 1637 Gov. John Sanford of Providence, his second wife. 

His Will was proved in 1653.

CLOVIS, the first king of all the Franks, born A. D. 466 was baptized at Rheims A. D. 496, and died in 511. He married Saint

Clothilde of Burgundy, "The Girl of the French Vineyards," who led him to embrace Christianity. When Clovis first listened to the story of Christ's crucifixion he was so moved that he cried, "If I had been there with my valiant Franks, I would have avenged Him."

Thomas Fiennes, 9th Lord Dacre, born 1515, one of the jury at the trial of Anne Boleyn, 1536, who also bore the canopy at the funeral of Jane Seymour in 1538.

On the eve of May Day 1541, when less than twenty-six years of age, Thomas Fiennes, Lord Dacre, was unfortunately "tempted by his own folly or that of his friends to join a party to kill deer" in the park of an unpopular neighbor. They were seen by the foresters and a fray ensued in which one of the keepers was killed. The charge was indeed serious: manslaughter following deer stealing, which in itself was a felony. Both he and his friends were general favorites, and the privy council hesitated long before they adjudged him guilty, being convinced that “if a poor man must be sent to the gallows for an act into which he might have been tempted by poverty, thoughtlessness could not be held as an excuse because the offender was a peer." King Henry, remaining true to his principles of equal justice, did not intervene, and Thomas was hanged at Tyburn 29 June 1541, whereby it was considered that his honors were forfeited. He was buried in St. Sepulchre's Church near Newgate. 

He had two sons: Thomas, who died at the age of fourteen years, and Gregory, Lord Dacre, who died without issue in 1593, and a daughter Margaret Fiennes, of whom later. These children happily were restored in blood, estate and honors by Queen Elizabeth. Thomas, 9th Lord Dacre, married (12) Mary Nevill, who was descended as follows:

The Houses of Howard and Arundel were by no means peaceful clans. They were definitely with the King or against him, most of the time against him, which was true of Sir 

Thomas Arundel. 

12. Sir Matthew Arundel of Wardour, who fled to the Continent, assumed the maiden name of his mother, wandered over Europe and died there in 1598, having married Margaret, daughter of Sir Henry 

Willoughby of Wollaton, co. Nottingham. 

11. Sir Thomas Arundel "Howard," elder son, 1st Baron Arundel of Wardour, passed his early life on the Continent and served in the Imperial Hungarian Army against the Turks during the latter part of the 16th Century. He distinguished himself in battle, and as a reward for his bravery Rudolph II, Emperor of Germany, created him a Count of the Holy Roman Empire. The patent of creation, dated 

Prague 14 December 1593, conferred the title upon "you, Thomas, and all and every one of your children, heirs and legitimate descendants of both sexes already born or that ever hereafter shall be born." Thus the warrant conferred the title not only on the eldest son but also on every son and daughter and their descendants.

Sir Thomas Arundel Howard died 7 November 1639, having married second, 1 July 1608, Ann Philipson, died 28 June 1637, daughter of Miles Philipson and his wife Barbara Sandys. Being at odds with his noble kinsmen, he continued to use the surname Howard as his father had done. Harry W. Newman, in his Ancestry of Matthew 

Howard, relates how their eldest son

In Nesbit's Heraldry, Volume II, is the following comment: 

Simon de Orrock is without question the ancestor of the House of Orrock of that ilk in the county of Fife, reputed an ancient family and an honorable one. Sir Simon de Orrock's name is inscribed upon the Ragman's Roll, which for antiquity is the rival of the British 

Domesday Book.

The name of Orrick or Orrock is said to have originated from the rock upon that part of the Fife coast where lay the large estate of Orrock. A history of the Orrocks of Scotland, whose arms continue to be borne by the Orricks of America, takes us back to the 13th

1880 to 1913 he was a merchant and owned farms and in 1887 helped to organize the Citizens' Bank of Weston and was on the Board of Directors until his death in 1934. He was on the first Board of

B. Francis John Saverline married Minnie Greer and had (1) Helen Saverline; (2) Esther Saverline; (3) Earl Saverline; (4) Norma Saverline; (5) Clifford Saverline. *2. Alice May Saverline, C. above, born 26 May 1889, married 14 

February 1907 William LaVerne Cornelius, born 15 May 1887, son of 

William Riley Cornelius and his wife Clara Louisa Strickland, who was born in 1853, daughter of Francis Strickland, born at Sherbourne, England (American Civil War Veteran) and his wife Catherine Louisa Camp, a descendant of Nicholas Camp I and John Rogers. Nicholas 

Camp was one of the founders of Milford, Connecticut, in 1639. Other ancestors were Henry Bottsford, Timothy Baldwin, and Nathaniel (H)Eaton, who came to Boston in 1634 and was made a Freeman in 1639. 

The CORNELIUS family has been eminent through the ages for Christian faith and services. The name dates back to B. C. 212 and is one of the oldest in genealogical records. In "Josephus" we find one "Publius Cornelius," second in command of the Roman Army. He was sent to Spain to fight against Hasdrubel, brother of Hannibal, and was killed in battle B. C. 212. Later one of his descendants was "Cornelius, Bishop of Rome" and was called the 21st Pope. He was exiled and martyred A. D. 253. The coat-of-arms bears ermine fur, signifying royalty, and chevrons, suggestive of Divine Protection.

Alice May Cornelius is now Mrs. P. R. Gaskill and is a life mem ber of The National Society Magna Charta Dames (Chaplain of West

Texas Colony); Order of Eastern Star, #447, Odessa; White Shrine of Oklahoma, highest Order of religious work in O.E.S. She has one daughter, of whom we treat: 

*1. DORIS VIOLET CORNELIUS, born at Bradford, Pennsyl vania, 6 December 1907, educated privately and in the public schools there, and later in Ardmore, Oklahoma. On 28 February 1929 she married Estill Carl Reece who holds an executive position with Shell 

Pipe Line Corporation, having offices in Odessa and Midland, Texas. 

He will retire soon, with thirty-five years of service. He is a 32° Mason; 

Shriner of El Maida Temple, El Paso, Texas; Member of the Odessa 

Chamber of Commerce; and past "Wagon Boss" of the well-known "Odessa Chuck Wagon Gang," who travel in their own planes and buses all over the Nation, serving Western barbeque to as many as 18,000 persons at one time. The couple have one foster daughter, Juanita Williams Wofford of Allen, Oklahoma, who is the mother of: a. Winfred Earl Wofford; b. Billye Doris Wofford; c. Harold Ray Wofford; d. Garry Dean Wofford; e. Roy Len Wofford.

They are eligible through their paternal lineage for various hereditary Societies.

Mrs. Reece has devoted her life to philanthropic work and has held responsible positions in the First Methodist Church, of which she has been a member for more than thirty years. She is also active in the following: Creative Writers Guild: Ladies' Oriental Shrine of North America, El Kantara Court #70, Midland, Texas; Order of Eastern Star #447, Odessa; American Natural History Associa tion; Odessa Civic Music Association; Federated Grandmothers Club of America, #208; and holds life membership in Nathaniel Davis

Chapter of Daughters of The American Revolution; (Chairman of National Defense); Daughters of Union Veterans, Orilla Shearer Tent, #14, Houston; National Society of New England Women (State Chairman); The National Society Magna Charta Dames (Colony

*1. MILDRED ANN DODSON SEITZ, (b) above, assumed the management of her father's lumber business and at his death became sole owner. She is the only woman member of the Railway Tie

At the moment she is collaborating with her husband on a book concerning guerrilla activities during the Civil War. She is lecturing on Laos and compiling material on that little-known country, preparatory to a series of articles.

Both Mr. and Mrs. Tomlin were pharmacists and owned drug stores in Texas until their retirement in 1929, when they moved to 

Dallas. There they originated and manufactured "Marie Tomlin

Cosmetics." After the death of her husband Mrs. Tomlin became 

President of "Marie Tomlin, Incorporated," and continued the business until retirement in 1949.

Mrs. Tomlin is a life member of The National Society Magna 

Charta Dames, the Society of Americans of Royal Descent, The Plantagenet Society, Dames of the Court of Honor, Society of Descendants of Knights of the Garter and Daughters of the American 

Revolution. 

They were the parents of two children: (a) Daniel Otis Tomlin, born 14 February 1915, a graduate of 

Southern Methodist University, Dallas, Texas, and Harvard

School of Business Administration. He also attended Northwestern University, Evanston, Illinois, and Washington University, St. Louis, Missouri. He married 4 June 1938 Erline 

Schuessler, born 10 June 1913, also a graduate of Southern

Methodist University. During World War II Mr. Tomlin was assistant manager of a War Industry, American Lead and 

Zinc Company of Dumas, Texas, and St. Louis, Missouri. A

Prisoner of War Camp was located at Dumas on the premises of the American Lead and Zinc Company at that time. This manufacturer of raw materials from which ammunition was made, employed prison labor from this camp. Later, Mr. 

Tomlin was President of the Dearborn Stove Manufacturing

Company. In 1956 he was elected President of the Dallas 

Manufacturers and Wholesalers Association, and in 1958 

elected State President of Texas Manufacturers Association. 

He is now and has been for several years President of the 

Lone Star Boat Company, with plants at Dallas, Texas, Tallahassee, Florida, Hazleton, Pennsylvania, and Bramen, Indiana.

Mr. Tomlin is a life member of the Society of Americans of Royal Descent, Somerset Chapter Magna Charta Barons, an hereditary member of The Plantagenet Society and a member of the Sons of the American Revolution. He and his family are members of the Highland Park Methodist Church of Dallas, where he serves on the Board of Stewards. They are the parents of: (1) Daniel Otis Tomlin, Jr., born 23 May 1943, an hereditary member of the Society of Americans of Royal

14. Anne Knyvett married Richard Sayre, who was born at Colchester, co. Essex, in 1508, and died in Holland in 1540, having fled there to escape the religious persecutions of King Henry VIII. He was the son of John Sayres of Colchester, who died in 1562. Richard denied the spiritual supremacy of King Henry VIII and was therefore exiled with his wife in 1537. She incurred the lasting displeasure of the 

Knyvett family, for she clung faithfully to her husband, and consequently her name was erased from the family pedigree and papers. 

Their only child 13. John Sayre was born in 1528 and married Elizabeth Hawkins, born 1532, died 1595, daughter of Admiral Sir John Hawkins, the renowned navigator.

In 1585 he married Marie Lamoral Van Egmonte, daughter of Count Philip Lamoral Van Egmonte of Amsterdam, and acquired a large fortune through this marriage. The elder of their two sons 

11. Richard Sayre (Sears) was born in 1590 and died at Yarmouth, Massachusetts, 26 August 1676. He came into his inheritance in 1629 and in 1630 joined the Company at Leyden and came to Plymouth, Massachusetts, with the last of the famous Scrooby Congregation. He first appears on the tax list there in 1633 and was awarded a grant of land at Salem in 1638. He was Captain of Militia in the Narragansett War in 1645. In 1662 he was deputy to the General 

Court and was a founder of Yarmouth. He married in England 

Dorothy Thacher, who was born in 1614 and died at Yarmouth 19 

March 1678/9.

1721, daughter of George Willard and his wife Dorothy Dunster of

Scituate, Massachusetts. Paul Sears was Captain of Militia in the 

Narragansett War, a grand juror in 1677 and was an original proprietor of Harwich, Massachusetts.

Elizabeth Ryland. (9) Colonel William Randolph as above married *9 Mary Isham and had *8. Thomas Randolph who, in 1712 married second Judith 

Fleming, daughter of Colonel Fleming. *7. Mary Isham Randolph, born 1718, died 1772, married in 1733 the Reverend James Keith, who was born in Scotland in 1696 and died in Prince William County, Virginia, in 1758.

The Keith family of Virginia descend from the Mareschals of the 

Scottish Army under Bruce. George Keith, born at Kincardine, Scotland, in 1685, who died near Potsdam, Prussia, 25 May 1778, was the 10th and last Earl to bear the name. His family had long been 

Mareschals of Scotland and were in possession of large estates. The family were adherents of the Stuarts and took an active part in the Rebellion in 1715, in favor of the Pretender. Alexander and James 

Keith, afterward Field Marshals of Russia and Prussia, were younger brothers of the Earl.

James Keith I was a Professor in the Marschal College at Aberdeen, Scotland. He was also a Bishop of the Episcopal Church and the uncle and guardian of the Earl and his brothers. His grandson James II (the Parson) had been educated with his cousins and, in 1715, was nineteen years of age. The Earl and his brothers took part in the 

Rebellion and were forced to escape to the Continent. Here, with the help of their cousin James at home, they continued to incite discontent and, in 1719, reentered Scotland but were repulsed. When the part which their cousin James Keith II had taken was discovered, he took refuge in the Colony of Virginia. He later returned to England to be ordained a Minister in the Church of England. He was Pastor of Old St. John's Church, Henrico County, Virginia, where Patrick 

Henry made his famous speech. He also ministered in Hamilton 

Parish, Fauquier County. Their second son was *6. John Keith of Fauquier County, born 1735, died intestate 

1809. He served in the War for Independence in Colonel Coxe's 

Regiment of Militia in Jefferson County, Virginia, and also furnished supplies for the Army. He married in 1755 Mary Elizabeth Doniphan, sister of "Old Doctor Doniphan," and daughter of Joseph Doniphan; and their ten children are listed as follows in Fauquier County records, Bill in Suit, 24 July 1834: (1) Alexander; (2) Anderson; (3) George; (4) Joseph; (5) Judith; (6) Elizabeth; (7) Susan; (8) Peyton 

Randolph (No. *5 below); (9) Thomas R.; and (10) Doniphan.

The 1790 Census includes the names of James and John Keith, and it is said that they were the only persons of the name listed in Virginia at that time. *5. Peyton Randolph Keith, No. 8 above, born in Fauquier 

County, Virginia, 20 June 1778, died at Amherst County, Virginia, 13 October 1842, married 18 May 1803 Sarah Lucy Petty, who was born in Orange County, Virginia, and died 3 October 1865.

56. BRAN, King of Siluria, was commander of the British fleet. 

In the year A. D. 36, he resigned the crown to his son Caradoc and became Arch-Druid of the college of Siluria, where he remained some years until called upon to be a hostage for his son. During his seven years in Rome, he became the first royal convert to Christianity, and was baptized, it is said, by the Apostle Paul, as was his son Caradoc and the latter's two sons, King Cyllinus and Cynon. He is known as "Bran the Blessed Sovereign," as "he was the first to bring the faith of Christ to the Cymry." His recorded proverb is: "There is no good apart from God." He introduced the use of vellum into Britain. His son 

55. CARADOC (Caractacus) "one of nature's noblemen," was

King of Saluria (Monmouthshire, etc.) where he died. He was born at Trevan, Llanilid, in Glamorganshire. His valiant services to his country in connection with the attempted invasions of the island are well known. 

54. Cyllin (Cyllinus) King of Saluria, was sainted by the early

Church of Britain. "He first of the Cymry gave infants names, for before names were not given except to adults, and then from something characteristic in their bodies, minds or manner." 

53. Prince Coel, son of Cyllin, King of Siluria. In his day, about the year 170, Iranaeus wrote: "Christianity has been propagated among the Germans and the Britons." 

52. LLEUVER MAWR (The Great Light, or Lucius the Great) 

was the second Blessed Sovereign (Cadwalader was the third). King of Britain, he was baptized at Winchester by his father's first cousin, the younger St. Timothy, who suffered martyrdom at age 90 on 22

August A. D. 139. In A. D. 170 Lucius succeeded to the throne of 

Britain and became the first Christian king in all the world. He built the Cathedral at Llandaff, the first Christian sanctuary in Britain, and changed the established religion of Britain from Druidism to 

Christianity. 

48. CONSTANTINE THE GREAT (Flavius Valerius Aurelius 

Constantinus) born 265, died in May, A. D. 337, buried in the church of the Holy Apostles in Constantinople. Of British Birth and education, he is known as the first Christian Emperor. With a British army he set out to put an end to the persecution of Christians forever. The greatest of all Roman Emperors, he annexed Britain to the Roman Empire and founded Constantinople. In the year 321 he decreed that the Christian Sunday be truly observed as a day of rest, a wonderful boon to the toiling serfs. 

47. Constantius II, Emperor, who died 360. He married second

Faustina, conferred upon her the title of Augusta and by her had Constantia, wife of the Emperor Gratian (367-383) and her sister 

46. Theodora, the mother of 

45. Constantius III, the commander-in-chief of the Emperor Honorius' forces, who was later proclaimed Emperor, reigned only seven months and died in 421. In the year 410 the Roman army left Britain, never to return. About the year 432 Saint Patrick, a Scot named Succat, who had been a British slave, kidnapped by the Irish, escaped and later made his way back to Ireland as a missionary of the Gospel. With trumpet and drum he drew the people to him and is said to have won the entire Island. About a century later Saint Columba carried the gospel to Scotland and founded the Scottish church. Later Saint 

Boniface of Devonshire, England, carried the gospel to Germany and was there slain in A. D. 755. No land has ever received the gospel except it was brought there by some foreign missionary. 

Constantius married Galla Placidia, widow of Athaulf.

*2. Emily Heard Davis of Newton County, Georgia, born 1849, died 1927, married 14 December 1872 Walter Crawford Stevens, born 1845, died 1916. He was sixth in descent from Walter Stevens and his wife Ann Hearle and ninth in descent from Thomas Libby and his wife Jane Pomeroy, all of co. Cornwall, England.

Henry Stevens, the father of Walter Crawford Stevens, came to America in 1831 and became a lumberman and manufacturer of clay products on his large holdings in Greene and Baldwin Counties, Georgia. On 26 January 1839 he married Matilda, daughter of John 

Stephens and Martha his wife, of Wake County, North Carolina.

During the War between the States his Company supplied the Confederate Government with many sorely needed articles. As a consequence of this the plant was completely destroyed by Sherman on his march through Georgia. Henry Stevens was a Master Mason and a Methodist. His eldest son,

Walter Crawford Stevens, was educated at Emory College at Oxford, Georgia, where he was a member of the Few Literary Society. 

At the age of 17 he enlisted in the Confederate Army, in the 27th Georgia Battalion, for the duration. After the close of active hostilities he returned to Baldwin County and formed a partnership with his brother, John Henry, and uncle, William Stevens, late of England, for the manufacture of clay products, a pioneer in this business in the South. He was also a promoter and the first president of the 

Citizens National Bank in Macon, Georgia. He founded the H. Stevens 

Sons Company for the manufacture of clay products in Macon, Georgia, and the Oconee Brick and Tile Company of Milledgeville, Georgia. 

He was a philanthropist, a Methodist and a Democrat. Their daughter, 

*1. MARIE STEVENS, was born 9 Steptember 1883 at the home of her maternal grandparents, Wilson Lumpkin Davis and his wife Mary Wright, in Newton County, Georgia. She attended the Lucy 

Cobb Institute in Athens, Georgia, continuing her education traveling in Europe for nine months. She was in London for the Coronation of 

King Edward VII, and was presented, in audience, to Pope XIII in

Rome. On her return from Europe she made her debut in Macon 

Society. Two years later, 7 November 1905, she married Billington 

Sanders Walker, III, born at Monroe, Georgia, 3 April 1883, died 22

May 1913, and they had a son, Billington Sanders Walker, IV. The royal and baronial ancestry of the Walker family is recorded later in this Chapter. 

Marie Stevens (Mrs. Walker) married second at the Church of the Transfiguration in New York City, 7 July 1929, William Thomas 

Wood, II, who was born at Sanford, Florida, 11 October 1889, died 30 April 1959. He was of royal and baronial descent through the 

Dent family of Charles County, Maryland, and the Hinton family of 

Virginia and Georgia.

Marie Stevens Walker Wood was the first Chairman of Flower Show Judges accredited by the National Council of Garden Clubs of 

America; on the Board of the Garden Club of Georgia; one of the organizers and President of the Flower Arrangers' Club of Georgia; a Camellia judge, accredited by the American Camellia Society. She originated and conducted the Flower Arrangement Contest of the American Camellia Society for seven years. An accredited judge of the 

American Iris Society, she conducted the arrangement contest of that Society for two years. She was the first woman to receive the Distinguished Service Plaque of the American Camellia Society. This was awarded at the annual convention in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1955. 

Marie Stevens Walker Wood is the author of "Flower Arrangements 

Judged and Point Scored" (foreword by John Taylor Arms). This book received the Award of Merit of the Garden Club of Georgia at the convention in Augusta, Georgia, in 1952. She edited three issues of "Artistry in Arrangement," published by the Flower Arrangers' Club of Georgia. "The Old and New in Flower Arranging," a resumé of a lecture and flower arrangement demonstration was given by Mrs. 

Wood on the sixth Garden Symposium at Williamsburg, Virginia, in 1954. 

Mrs.

Wood was co-author with William Thomas Wood of "Flower 

Show Know How." "The Walker Heritage" and "Stevens-Davis and

1. BILLINGTON SANDERS WALKER, III, born at Monroe, 

Georgia, 3 April 1883, died 22 May 1913, as above married 7 Novem ber 1905 *1 Marie Stevens. 

He attended Johnston Institute, the Griffin High School and was graduated from the University of Georgia in 1903 (Sigma Alpha 

Epsilon Fraternity). He was cashier of the First National Bank of 

Barnesville, Georgia. Removing to Monroe, he was President and owner of the Walton Trading Company. He founded the Company: 

B. S. Walker, Real Estate and Loans, in which he was active at the time of his death at the age of 30 years. He is buried in the family burying ground at Monroe, where his ancestors have been buried since the War for Independence. 

Mr.

Walker was a member, among other organizations, of the 

First Baptist Church, the Benevolent and Protective Order of Elks and the Idle Hour Country Club. 

Billington Sanders Walker, III, and his wife Marie Stevens had an only son 

* BILLINGTON SANDERS WALKER, IV, who was born at the Sidney Lanier Cottage 7 May 1909. This historic home was owned by Mr. Walker's family for more than forty years. He was graduated with honors from the Lanier High School and from the University of Georgia in 1930 (A.B. Cum Laude); Phi Beta Kappa. He was later graduated with distinction from the Babson School of Business Administration at Wellesley, Massachusetts. He served as a Lieutenant in the United States Navy from November 1943 to 1945, participating in the Invasion of Peleliu.

Macon; past President, Macon Association of Insurance Agents; member of the Executive Committee of the Georgia Association of Insurance Agents; Vice President, Macon Base Ball Company (pennant

Epsilon Fraternity, 1958.

Order of the Crown and The Plantagenet Society. (See Who's Who in Commerce and Industry, Eleventh International Edition.)

*30. Elise (Hesilia) Crispin married WILLIAM, LORD MALET, died 1072, called grandson of GODIVA. He was a Norman Baron, a general and companion of William the Conqueror, and is said to have been the brother of King Harold's wife and to have been entrusted with the guard of Harold's body after he was slain on the battlefield of Hastings. After the conquest he was made governor of York Castle and was slain in its defense. Their second son was *29. Gilbert Malet, whose brother Robert, Lord Malet, was great

According to an old pedigree: "The family of the Kynnersleys is very ancient, being seated long before the Conquest in com. Hereford, in a castle soe called at present. In Doomesday Booke it is recorded that when the Conqueror was possessed of his newe Kingdome of England, hee sent his Comissrs throughout ye remote parts thereof, to know howe every man held his lands. In which tyme there was an ould gentleman that lived and was owner of Kynnardsley Castle, in com. Hereford: by name John de Kynnardsley, and by title a knight 

(if any knights were before the Conquest). This ould gentleman was blind, he had then liveing with him twelve sonnes, whom with himself he armed, and stood in his castle gate, his halberd in his hand, attending the coming of the sheriffs and other comissrs from ye king, who being arrived, demanded of him by what tenure he held his castle and lands; ye old knt replyed: by his armes, showing to them his halberd."

They are descendants of the distinguished family of Connor of Dublin, Ireland; and there is extant an interesting illustration of the Arms of O'Connor Faly taken from one of the gate posts on the O'Connor Estate. The Arms were in concealment for nearly 400 years. They belonged to the family of that name of the principality of Offaly in Leinster. This family never yielded to the British and were strong in support of the old Irish culture. Consequently they were destroyed by the British in the latter part of the 16th Century.
